div.head: WHEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WHEN'S CHAT.

Royal Visitors for Cheshire.—The King is to visit the Duke and Duchess of Westminister at Eaton Hall next week for the Chester races. The last occasion on which his Majesty attended the Chester meeting was nine years ago, when, as Prince of Wales, he was the guest of Colonel and Mrs. Cornwallis West, at Ruthin Castle. On this occasion their daughter, the Duchess of Westminster, will aet as hostess to King Edward, nod there wilt b 3 a large party at Eaton Hall for the Royal visit, and for the races. A little later on Royalty will again he enter- tained at Eaton Hall, for the opening of Stockport Town Hall. The Prince and Princess of Wales are to perform the ceremony, on July 7th, ank their Royal Highnesses will be the guests of the Duke and Duchess of Westminster for two or three days at Eaton Hall. Eaton Hall.—The Duke of Westminster's seat is about 4 miles from Chester, and is one of the finest ducal residences in the kingdom. The late Duke began the building of Eaton Hall in 1837, on the site of the original homestead of the Grosvenors, and it was the great undertaking of his life. It took fourteen or fifteen years to complete, and it was during the building of this most palatial mansion of modern times, that the Marquis of Westminster was created a duke. in after -years be had a granite column erected in the nark,which is known as the" Secret Monument," and it is under- steed to be the memorial of a vow made by the late Duke when he parted from Mr. Gladstone, and the Liberal party. There is a smaller house attached to Eaton Hall, in which the Duke and Duchess reside when not entertaining on a large scale, and it is only on occasions of Royal visits, of the entertaining of a Urge house party, that Eaton Hall is thrown open in all its princely magnificence. Monuments to Women—The Oaicla monument by which it is proposed to commemorate the famous novelist, will make a notable addition to the very few existing monuments to women, apart from Royal personages. That to Mrs. Siddon is the only one in London, if we except the Baadicea monument, at Westminster, which however commemorates the courageons and militant woman, rather than her character as queen. There are but three other statues to women in Britain, Flora Macdonald at Inveiness ; Highland Mary at Dunoon ; and Sister Dora at Walsall. Probably at some future time there will be one to acknowledge the debt of humanity to Florence Nightingale, but as yet we have not got as far in this direction as the United States, which has placed a memorial window to the Crimean heroine, in the chapel of Cornell University. In the nursing section of the - Women's Palace at the Franco-British Exhibition, there will be the carriage on view in which Florence Nightingale did most of her travelling in the Crimea. Women Dentists.—At the present time there would appear to be only about six or seven women dentists on the register, and therefore a good opaoing in this direction seems to lie before es. It is true that although

_ allowed to take out our lectures in any of the dental schools, we are only admitted to the Scotch diploma, the London College of Surgeons refusing us this honour : still sufficient way is open to the aspirant. The training for women is the same as for man, an 4 both =IA register as students in London, the average cost being about £250, and the minimum time fain. years. Needless to say, the woman dentist must he cosseted of excellent health, for the life is a hard and trying one, although perhaps not quits so mach as that of the woman doctor.

—.— Vegetables and Fruit Desirable.—Spinach is a vegetable one should partake freely of, a fact well- known to the most enlightened "beauty specialists,"who strongly advise for their "patients" at least one liberal helping daily. Spinach is excellent for the liver, and as a consequence freshens the complexion. Onions too, plainly boiled, have a brightening and clearing effect on the complexion, and should be partaken of freely. They are useful too, in cases of nervous prostration, and greatly assist in giving to the system. Fewer girls and women would have to complain of spots, and muddy skins, if less meat, and " made dishes ' were indulged in. and more vegetables and ripe fruit consumed, especi- ally at this season of the year. Open Windows and the Fly Nuisance.—For yearn the doctors have preached the doctrine of the " open window" and yet it has been discovered that the great majority of the houses of the leading London physicians habitually remain closed. Then again, the London County Council conducted same experiments last year to test the extent of the common fly nuisance, and found that houses with windows kept open were much more infested with lie s than was the case in others where they were kept shut. YlieS feed qpon filth and refuse, and come from their feeding piaces faa ae sugar basin and milk jug. Wherever they are, theta is the danger of infection, but one can have bat little faith in snccess of any organised eff9rts to exterminate them, That seems out of the question, althaag,la it is talitr,d about by sanitary authorities, and it almost looks as if we shall have to sacrifice another cherished institution —hat, 7ir—when, an the summer.tirne, it Is most needed.

.2aohl!t.—We ars accsiorned to sachots sewn into our bodices, skirts, underskirts, wraps, boas and head- gear, but the sachet hatpin is a distinct novelty. The heads of these new pins are stuffed with perfumed wadding, and covered with knitted silk, plain colours being in better taste 'than mixtures. The girl who possesses a pin from which the knob has departed—the metal cup still rernaining—shcaild find -it an easy matter Inske up a sachet hat-pin, ordinary wadding being goodly heap of 11(7 ritilisei £2 which onew,ju a favourite perfume powder. Instead thetefOre of a quick change from the simple schoolroom " tie back," to the elaborate twists, . coils, and curbs of the dZsbutante there is now an intermediate stage, in which the hair is Coaxed into the ways to come. And even when simply tied back, different methods are resorted to day by day, so that the hair raay not make for itself part- • logs, or show inclinations to lie in any particular way. Fashionable mothers are insisting that the broad ribbons • which tie back their young deneaters' hair shall exactly match their tresses, shot effects being sought

There is no better place in England for a HOLIDAY than DEVON or CORNWALL. The charming scenery of the two counties, the lovely coast line mud rugged moorlands, combined with mild and equable cli:uate, constitute a RIVIERA of which England has reason to be proud. In no other part of the United Kingdom is there such diversity of scenery and such charm of surroundings for all in search of rest, change and sunshine.

Send for one or both of the high-class travel books : " DEVON : THE SHIRE OF THE SEA KINGS." and "THE CORNISH RIVIERA." These useful, holiday-planning publications are beautifully illustrated and well written, and may bc obtained from the Superintendent of the Line, G.W.R., Paddington Station, W., for postage 3d. each; from whom may also be obtained full particulars of the cheap week-end, excursion and tourist fares.

Another Anglo-American Engagament.—Lord Dudley is to accompany the Prince of Wales on his visit to Canada next July, and will go from there to take up his post as Governor-General of Australia, but the Countess wilt not follow until some weeks later. Mean- while there is to be another wedding in the family, that of the Hon. John Ward, who is engaged to Miss Jean Whitelaw Reid. the only daughter of the United States Ambassador. The Hon. John Ward. who is thirty-eight years of age, is the second of the five sons of Geerg,iana Countess of Dudley, and is the only unmarried brother of the present earl. It will be one of the great Society weddings of the season, as Mr. and Mrs. Whitelaw Reid are accustomed to entertain on a princely scale at Dorchester House, and their daughier is very popular in London. Mr. and Mrs. Whitelevy Reid are immensely rich, and have one son, but of course it will be said on the other side that it is a case of yet another American heiress marrying into the British aristocracy. Usirg Up the Scraps.—An excellent way in which to utili3e scraps of cold boiled fish, is as follows :—Butter a pie dish and place at the bottom the fish, flaked, and free from bone. Upon this dust a little pepper and salt, and several spoonfuls of white sauce. (A few knobs of butter can be substituted for the sauce if preferred.) Then arrange a layer of mashed potato, and upon this a few breadcrumbs, place in a quick oven for half an hour, and serve. MADGE.

div.head: P.S A. Meetings.
div.p: P.S A. Meetings.

At the weekly meeting, of the Wycliffe P.S.A.. held on Sunday under the presidency of the Secretary, Mr. Cance, of Newton Heath, gave an address upon "Hymns and hymn writers." He related a few inci- dents in the life of composers of various hymns, and referred especially to Cowper, who suffered -much from depression. Yet he could give to the world such helpful words and thoughts.—Miss Povey sang sweetly " I know that my Redeemer liveth " and "Sun of my Soul." Mr. W.H. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. Gleave also took part in the meeting. Two new members rt:.Teived a hearty welcome. The Brother- Bow nrokrs 417. A letter of thanks to the ' re taren was wtad from Hr. J. Walley, of Manchester, who had received a fe::!Ar of congratulation for him• self and wife, upon reaching ,oz.ir golden wedding.— There was was a very good attendance at the . ing of the Warrington Society on Sunday. The at,,441" dent occupied the chair, and spoke upon " The joy of true living and the satisfaction derived from self- sacrfice." An address was delivered by Mr. Holland on " The call to service." Prayer was offered by Mr. T. Taker, and the lesson was read by Mr. Brown. The musical part of the meeting was supplied hy the orchestra. A. vote of condolence was passed with 4. Walker whose wife has recently died.

div.p: ROYAL OPINIONS' ON SUFFRAGETTES.

Though Queen Alexandra wisely refrains from publicly influencing politics in any way her sym- pathies are certainly not with the suffragist cause, declares the Tatler. Her Majesty has herself always shewn by her example how woman's power is best and most potently wielded from her own domain. This opinion is shared by the Princess of Wales. Queen Vic- toria 'writing on the subject of "women's rights" and those who raised the agitation on lie subject thirty-eight years ago says: " The Queen is most anxious to enlist everyone who can speak o,r write in checking this mad folly of women's ,rights with all its attendant horrors on which her poor feeble sex is bent, forgetting every sense of womanly feeling and propriety. Lady ought to get a good whipping. It is a subject that makes the Queen so furious that sho cannot contain herself." The lady whose sudden and conspicuous appearance on public platforms elicited this protest from Queen Vic- toria in 1870. was a young matron who bore ft highly-honoured name and was afterwards per- sonally remonstrated with by the Queen.

div.head: HYACINTH – BLUE EOLIENNE COSTIEVE.
div.p: HYACINTH - BLUE EOLIENNE COSTIEVE.

There was never a time when dress was so pic- turesque in so many styles to suit all tastes and figures. A pretty example of a prevailing mode is shown in our sketch, where a dross of hyacinth-blue eolierme is depicted. The full skirt has a narrow pleat or panel down the front, decorated with small buttons covered with blue taffetas. The bodice is arranged with tucks on

the shoulders, the fulness being draped to the centre beneath the short strap, which gives the effect of a continuation of the panel of the skirt. It finishes in a Point at the yoke, and is also de- corated with buttons. The yoke and armholes are bordered with Oriental trimming, embroi- dered in subdued shades of blue. The loose cape-like sleeves are finished with small tucks, and fall over under-sleeves of old ivory-tinted net. A guimpe of the same net and some thick patterned lace fills in the opening at the neck. A WAY OF DANGER.

We do not seem sufficiently to realise that we are giving too much place to ugliness nowadays, writes " Ambrosia " in the World. A writer in one of the review( laments our tendency in this direction, and threatens that we ourselves shall "grow so" unless we take a turn and devote our worship to the beautiful. It is our desperate anxiety to be realistic and indivsalistic that has brought about the condition of things of which complaint is made. While one is about it, it is 418 easy 0 be beautiful, to have beautiful surroundings, and to see beauty in all and sun- dry as to try to make the best of ugliness and persistently to see the seamy side. The artist who will wonderfully paint hideous peasant women, the writer who in the most vivid and masterly way shews us nothing but thp cruelty and hardness and viciousness of existence, the portrait-painter who gives us wonderful like- nesses in the most unpleasing manner, and the fashion-monger who skilfully treats the most bizarre modes and utiliies the most trying colours, are all to be condemned. They are in the majority nowadays. And if we continue on this fare we shall not grow snore beautiful.

div.head: :WRY ,THE SKY LOOKS BLUE.
div.p: :WRY ,THE SKY LOOKS BLUE.

The gas we call air is transparent and abso- lutely colourless. The blue comes from ,re- fleeted light. 'Air is never pure; you could not live in it if it were. Countless millions of tiny particles, chiefly of water, are always suspendod in it, and these arrest the free passage of light. Each particle has a double reflection—one in- ternal the other external—and so the reflected rays suffer the usual result of what is called "interference," and show colour. You will notice that the sky appears much bluer if you look straight up than if you look across towards the horizon. The reason is that in the first instance you are naturally looking through a much thinner layer of air than in the second. If there were no air, and consequently no watery vapour, and nothing to interfere with the free, passage of light, even at mid-day the sky above would look perfectly black, and all the stars plainer than they do now at mid- night. --- WORTH KNOWING.

Some interesting calculations were made te show why extra .ventilation is necessary at night when the room.] are lighted. That tha amount of oxygen in a room is decreased alarm. ingly by our methods of illumination the fol. lowing simple statements will show. A maxi may exist for an hour in a fair-sized room hermetically .sealcd if he has no light burning. Place a lighted candle in that room with him and his existence will be shortened by fifteen minutes. If he has a lamp instead of a candle in *order to make himself more comfortable with additional` light, he would live only half an hour. If he had two good gas burners be would scarcely have time to make his will, for he would not live more than five minutes.

div.p: NOVEL GAS LIGHTEP-.

A novel clockwork gas lighter has been in- vented by three brothers named Horstmann, of Bath. The contrivance is wound up weekly or fortnightly when the lamp it cleaned, and the clockwork arrangement not only puts the light on and turns it off, but does this at a different time every day in the year, according to the season, as the daylight lengthens or diminishes. Not only is the lamplighter nupereeded by this apparatus, which cods 355., but there is a saving in the gas mantles.

The Synod in connection with the Liverpool District of the Primitive Methodist Church, held at Warrington for the first time, resumed its deliberations at Legh- street Church on Saturday and Mon lay. The Rev. W. Spedding (Birkenhead) presided, and was accompanied by the Rev. W. W. Goldstraw (secretary). There ,vere large atcendances at all the meeting, and the proceed- ings were meet successful and helpful. The dis- triot includes 45 cirouits, ranging frum North Wales tri Cumberland. Reports on Christian Eudeavoer, Sunday school, chapel building and church member- ship were submitted and regarded as satisfac- tory. The following are the leading statistics:— members 10,633, increase 128 ; ministers 72 ; local preachers 74:5, increase 6 ; class leaders 559, increase 6 ; sabbath schools 199, increase 1 ; teachers 3,283, decreese 52; scholars 26,659, decrease 330 ; scholar members over 14 years, 3,102. increase 155 ; scholar members under 14 years, 2,713, decrease 20 ; connex. chapels, 201, increase 1 ; other preaching places 10, increase 1 ; hearers 31,925, decrease 359 ; value of connexioral property, £326,853! increase £5,427; debt on connexional property, £78,198, Increase £720. div.head: IMVCATION.
div.p: IMVCATION.

It was resolved : That this meeting representing 210 churches in Lancashire and Cheshire expresses its gratifi- cation at the introduction of Mr. McKenna's Education Bill an reaognizes it as a loyal fulfilment of the pledges given by H.M. Government on this great ques- tion. It especially appreciates the provision which the measure offers for rural educational emancipation and for freeing the teachers in elementary schools from sectarian tests and on condition that these great advan- tages are assured it offers no resistanc3 to other features of the Bill which, taken by themselves, are or 3n to serious objection. The meeting regards with approbation proposals now being made for a friendly eon ference of the representatives of conflicting interests but it must be distinctly understood that it will strongly oppose any attempt to introduce sectarianism into Council Schools and strongly urges that no State- paid teachers should' be allowed to give sectarian teaching. _ _

div.head: CONGO ATROC IT lES.
div.p: THE CONGO ATROC IT lES.

The Synod resolved: That this meeting denounces the system of exploitation introduced into the Congo Free Stato whereby the native population is subjected to most barbarous and inhuman conditions. It views with grave apprehension the proposed treaty of cession which retains intact the root causes of mal-administra- tion prevailing in that State. This meeting relies upon His Majesty's Government intimating to the Congo and Belgian Governments that this treaty, violating as it does,not only the tights of the natives but the treaty rights of this end other countries cannot be accepted by H.M. Government as a solution of the Congo question. STATIONS OF MINISTERS. . .

The Synod approved the list of stations of ministers for the year 1908-9. The local appointments are:— Warrington, Revs. J. B. Baglass and Jonathan Calvert ; Earlestown, Rev. Walter Tanley ; St. Helens, Rev. John Bradley; Preston Brook and Runcorn' Rev. W. Walter Goldstraw ; Widnes, Rev. S. George Delaliald.

What was there common to every one of those related movements which represented the ancestry of Primitive Methodism ? Jeers Christ preached and lived the great truth of the value of man in the sight of God. Jesus went to seek the outcast: He saw in the raw material in the slums of his own day the possibilities of an infinite man. Was not that the. meaning of the Reformation and of Puritanism ? As Macaulay had said, the Puriton was the mall who wanted to gaze upon God and realize God for himself. It was one of the paradoxes of Puritanism that the Puritan was at once the humblest and the proudest- man that lived, because he realized that he was of infinite value. Luther was the man who emancipated the individual soul and taught it its value with Jesus Christ. Wesley was the lover of men, and he said in a memorable sentenc 3 : " Church or no Church, we must save souls." After Wesley and the Evangelical movement came Hugh Bourne and William Clowes. Just before Primitive Methodism arose, there was a marvellous political movement—the French P wet:Lion. laey had nothing to do with party politics there, except so far as party politics were righteous, but they had to do with moral and spiritual politics, and there was a magnifi- cently religious side of the French Revolution, for the secret of it was the secret of Jesus " A man's a man for a' that." The current of the French Revolution was in them, and so on the political or ecclesiastical side of their movement they got Methodist New Connexionalism but on the spiritual, under-side of it they got revivalism, evangelism, Primitive IM ethodism. Not one had d word will I say against the Wesleyans. They were looking after the ideal of the Church for the time being. Primitive Methodism arose to give another assertion to the grand thought of the value of man as man asagainst Cuurch as Church. Man was not made for the Church, but the Church was made for man." There were, however, some things on which they could put their fingers and say with reasonable accuracy that " Primitive Methodism did something here." -Take, first of all, the influence Of Primitive Methodism on things peculiarly or entirely religious. Mr. Houghton hat not lived stood. (Applause.) amongst them for many years, but they could not over- - look the helpful work he did as a member of the Council for so many years. His Worship moved a vote of condolence with the widow and family in their sad loss. This was seconded by Alderman I'IERPOIST, and carried unanimously. ATTENDANCES AT CONFERENCES. Councillor EVANS having moved and Alderman Burerox having seconded the confirmation of the minutes of the Health Committee, Councillor STOTT alluded to the resolution that the Chairman and the Medical o.lleer beappointed to attend the annual conference of the Royal Sanitary Institute, to be held at Cardiff from the 13th to the 13th July. He objected, he explaiued," to the principle on which the deputations were appointed and to the opinion which appeared to exist that the chairman of a com- mittee should always be appointed, lie had no personal objection to the names and he admitted that no member of the Council worked harder than Councillor Evans worked, but other members of the Council should have en opportunity of attending these conferences and thus learning the work they had to do. He moved as an amendment that the minute be referred back to the committee. Counoillor SLZGLETOW seconded. Councillor EVANS explained that slam the death of the late chair nen of the committee (Alderman Sutton) and since he (Councillor Evans) had been appointed chairman he had not attended this particular confer- ence, lie was not anxious to go, and to prove that he stated that. he should have been in London that day on a deputation, but he had refrained from going to enable him to be present that evening. (Hear, hear.) He would leave the matter in the hands of the Cornell. (Ilear,hear.) Councillor Stott, On hearing this explanation, csLb drew his amendment. TRIBUTE TO THE HOSPITAL STAFF. '
SUNDAY SERVICES.

- - - --- On Smithy the ministers attending the Conference preached at various Free Churches in the towa. In the morning at Legli-street Church there was a crowded congregation, friends attending from Skelmersdale, St. Helens, Earlestown and surrounding districts. The preacher was the Rev. W. Upright, of Birkenhead, who based a powerful sermon on the words "We are labourers together with God." He said there was a sense lin which that was true of all men. They were workers together with God. He caused the wrath of men to praise Him and He made the wickedness of men work out his asll. in the Divine economy oven had men were inctuded and unconsciously they were working with. God. But, of course, St. Paul meant much more than this when he described himself and his fellow workers es laboureis with God. The words referred to a conscious and voluntary co-operation—to a willing and intelligent unity of purpose and effort in the will and work of God ; and they were particularly true of all who were engaged in any work which had real value and which ministered to human weal. No matter what their work might be they were labourers together with God in the highest and best sense, if the influence of their work was for good rather than evil, if it were a help and not a hindrance to the coming of his kingdom. It WO3 a very caustic critic who said that the peculiarity of the present day was that everybody wanted to reform the world end nobody dreamed of reforming himself. As Caristion workers they must see to it that such a charge wra not true as it concerned themselves. Reformation like charity began at home and unlers they had first of all begun by reforming themselves they would do little good in the world by reforms they proposed. At 1.45 there was anlopen-air service at Bridge-foot conducted by the Rev. J. Strong, with an address by Mr. H. Baker. At the close a procession was formed and proceeded to the vacant ground off Wilderspool- road where a camp meeting was held. Tne attendance numbered between COO and 700 and the service was very hearty and helpful. Mr. Spruce acted es precentor. The conductors were the Rev. J. Whittle and Mr. J. Tranter, and the preachers the Rev. W. Moore, Mr. IL Leach and Rev. E. Mather. In the evening a service was held in the Parr Hall and proved most successful, the congregation numbering about 1,000. The Rev. B. Fell conducted the proceedings and the preacher was the Rev. J. D. Thompson. His subject woe "Armageddon," the original meaning of which he cam• fully explained It represented the great battle ground of the Bible—where both victories and defeats were realised. It meent in the New Testament the war of Christ and anti-Carist. the Messiah and the world- monster. Toe word was dead as a word hut it repre- sented a living principle, for the fight between right and wrong, good and evil—in a word the battle of the ages—is always going on. me present Licensing Bill of the Government was instenced as a true "Armageddon." The chief point of the preacher wan that— Virtue's battle once begur Though baffled oft is ever Won, Bequeathed from blesding sire to son. He urged the congregation to remember that war was never ended, and to continue strenuously and vigilantly to fight for the right and against sin and wrong every- where. But there was always the encouragement that we wore so constituted tbat we were alwzvs tending to forget defeats, and to count only on victories for virtue and the right. The preacher applied his subject both to the fight against wrong in outward history, and to the struggle against sin in the individual soul ending with a stirring appeal to any who felt they neided help to turn to Christ for grace and salvation. The Choir of Legh-street Church gave an efitctive rendering of " Glorious is Thy Name" to the music of the Gloria in Mozart's 12th Mass. Mr. A. Spruce con- ducted and Mr: W. Clatworthy presided at the organ. At 7.45 there was one of the old-fashioned meetings for praise, prayer and testimony, a great number of those present bearing testimony to their religious experiences. The conductors were the Rev. B. Fell, Mr. T. Cuthbert end Mr. E. A. Sadler.

Councillor ROGERS said that on behalf of his nife and himself he wished to thank the Health Committee, Dr. Smith, Dr. Hilkert, Dr. Gaffikin, and the nurses at the Infectious Diseases Hospital for the great interest they lied taken on his daughter's behalf while a patient at the institution. He could not speak in too high terms of the manner in which the iestitution was con- ducted. He believed that if his daughter (who was suffering from typhoid fever) had not been sent to the hospital she would not have been alive that evening. She was restored and in good health. (Hear, hear). MEDICAL INSPECTION OF SCIIOOI4CFIILDREN. The Health Committee reported that the sub-corn-1 mittee appointed to consider the applicatiors received , for the position of Assistant Medical Officer of Health reported that in their opinion two assistant Medical , Officers were unnecescery, and that the work of school inspection could be r 3rformed by the resident Medical Officer at the Aikin-street Hospital, whilst the Medical Officer could take charge of the infectious cases, and that they recommended that the appointment should be again advertised, and that the salary be increseed to the sum of £l5O Per annum. Resolved, " Teat the Education Committee be requested to confer with his committee on the matter, and tbet the Town Clerk arrange an early meeting." Councillor SroTr said he could not understand why i the committee had taken this course after the under- standing arrieed at with the Education Committee. He, I however, strongly disagreed with the criticism offered in one local newspaper with regard to the recommenda- tion. He considered it was unfair, when the newspaper I itself admitted that it lacked the necessary information' on the subject. But what he was more concerned about than newspaper criticism was whether the work under the new Act was going to he carried out to the full ' extent. He did not want the Colleen to be satisfied with a minimum of inspection but to get as much out of the Act as possible. The Medical Officer had assured' him that the work of medical inspection under the scheme proposed with the Health Committee would not suffer, and that was by he had not carried out his intention to move that the matter be referred back for further consideration. Councillor EVAN'i said the resolution would never have appeared on the agenda bad it not been for the desire that there should be cohesion between the Education Committee and the Health Committee. I When they received the applications for the post of assistant medical officer they felt that they were not quite the quality of the medical men they expected would apply. They then went into the question of the ' desirability of appointing a resident medical officer at the Aikin-street Hospital to take care of about 30 children They did not want the person appointed for the school work to reside in the Aikin-street institution to deal with the infectious cases, but to attend to the serioua.crn which might arise during the night. They looked upon the risk they ran as very small, and if their critics would consider the question, as they ought, they would be conscious of the fact that from day to day every medical practitioner, or nearly so' went into the wards of the hospital and thence into the town generally. He did not say that to the detriment of the medical practitioners, who did their work under the best condi- tions. The late Dr. Gornall examined in connection with the schools 1,000 children, and Dr. Hibbert had examined 800. 'I here had been nothing effectually done so far as the Education Committee was con- cerned as the result of the examination. They bad no power to make provision for those who were found to be deficient. They could not carry the work further than the examination of the children. It was true that the sub-committee appointed by the Education Committee to deal with the matter were making proposals and adopting methods to see how far they could go, and how they might approach the Board of Education to enable them to spend money to deal with those physically unfit, but up to now no provision had been found and neither the Health Committee nor the Education Committee could spend money. They had exereined 1,800 and the whole question had not got one jot further, and why, therefore, should the Heelth Committee be forced to employ a second medical officer and charge the cost to the ratepayers, when in their judgment such an exr ease was absolutely unnecessary? RESIGNATION OF THE MATRON.

It was resolved at a meeting of the Health Com- mittee, that the resigo%tion of Miss Lees, mitron at the Aikin-street ilospitAl, be accepted. an tt-it she be allowed three months' salary. The minutes were then agreed to. BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVE TENT. DELAY COMPLAINED OF.

Alderman TINSION moved, and Councillor ETANVTUORN seconded, the confirmation of the ru'autes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee. Councillor &PICT:ETON asked for an explanation of the delay in the widening of the top of Bridge-street. This was not a persoral matter, but tradesmen were asking him the reason of the delay. With reference to the wood blocks the sf Jciacations were sent out correctly in the first place aud then it was found that they were an inch too big and fresh specifications hari to be sent out. Other blocks had been accented and, although not agreed to by the Council, Note being

" used. This was not the first time a similar occurrence had taken place, and he considered it was a disgrace. Alderman 3.‘INNION. in reply, said it was due to the chairman of a committee that some notice should be given of such questions. (Hear, hear.) He (the Alderman) was entitled to grumble because he had received no complaints at all about the work. As to Councillor Singleton's insinuations that .` this was not the first time," chapter and verse should have been given because, so far as he knew, the complaint was contrary to fact. It would also be better if newspaper writers would get their information from the Chairman of the Committee and then their statements would stand a little investigation. The work began at the top end of Bridge-street on March IL They had to pull down ' property. There were cellars right under the street which had to be filled, and it was difficult to form a permanent street, especially a street of the width of Bridge-street. He ventured to say that the wood paving that had been recently put down.—be referred to Sankey-street—would bear favourable comparison with that in many towns in England. (Hear, hear.) It was an admitted fact that if they wanted a good roadaSay they must have a good founda- tion. (Elear2 bear.) They had a good founda- tion, and at took them a little more time to nrepare it, and having got it they found they could do with a wood block one inch less, but it did not delay them an hour. He rather expected to have been con- gratulated on the work which had been done in Bridge- street, on the excellent job which had been made. (Hear, hear.) They were congratulated on the excellent manner in which the shops had been pulled down. The officials and himself had been congratulating each other upon the work having been done so well. (Hear, hear.) Some people seemed to think they could pull a place down and let the traffic go over the street at the same time. (Laughter.) He was not prepared to accept these insinuations, and he contended that there had been no delay and that the work bad been done well and expeditiously. He hoped that the next time a complaint was made there would be more foundation for it. (Hear, I hear.) The minutes were then passed.

div.head: ORDINATION SERVICE..
div.p: ORDINATION SERVICE..

On Mondaywe;:n-in the Synod with an ordina- tion service in Bold-street Church, at which there Nre a a large congregation. Councillor A. Roberts pre:sided, and Mr. A. R. Sadler occupied the vice-chair. The CHAIRMAN pointed out that the Cfmclidaf 3S for ordination were now about to begin a new life, and he appealed for the support of the congregations amongst whom they would labour to be extended to them. Man? congregations were too exacting in their demands, expecting the minister to preach and visit from Monday moiaing to Sunday evening, and then to trouble hin”elf about the finances of the Cnurch. It should also be understood that when they engaged a minister they did not engage his wife as well. If a woman did her duty there was plenty of work for her to do at home. If all people would go to Church to worship instead of to criticise tho mi,Dister the resn'ts would he far more encouraging. ill‘pplanse.) The VICE-CHA IRMAN said the ordination seri, ice was one of the most important tip vices of the Christian Church end the call of young men to tho ministry was the highest call and the greatest honour that Christ could bestow. The two main lines which ministers of Christ were called upon to take were to seek and to save the lost and to guard those whom they brought to the feet of Christ. Miss Bridge ring "When I survey " (Podinore),very creditably. The candidates—Revs. A. Wightman, IT Chamber- lain and S. Chesworth—then briefly. nai rated their Christian experiences and call to the ministry and were afterwards presented with Bibles by ore ir iv. J. B. Buglass. The Rev. J. WHITILE, in delivering the ordination charge congratulated the candidates on the high honour and privilege of being called by the great Head of the Church to the work of the ministry. lne grandest vocation in the world was that of a preacher, a God called, divinely anointed prciher. Wnatever spiritual gifts might have been neceesai y and profitable to the church at other times he was persua lc I that the gift of prophesy was the one that was needed now. This age wanted, and was prepared to receive, not the priest but the prophet, not the man who claimed to st•ord between God and them, and yid "no access to the heavenly Maher but through me" but the man who could teach the truth, and help them

div.head: Complaints of Delay.
div.p: Complaints of Delay.
SWISIMING BATH FOR GIRLS.

Upon the minutes of the Town gall, Parks, and Piths Committee coming up for confirmation, Councillor STOTT expressed regret that the committee had not arrived at a decision with regard to the provision of a swimming bath for girls. He hoped something would be done before winter.
Alderman BOLTON said what was being done could not be made public at present, but they would have something prepared by the time the hot weather coma.
FALSE ALARM.

Aldermho BURTON proposed the adoption of the minutes of the Fire Engine Committee, and said the recent false alarm cost the ratepayers £Bor 1..',9.11e hoped even yet the culprit would be brought to justice. Councillor BARTON seconded and the minutes were passed.
TEE COST OF ELECTRIC LIGHT. IS IT REASONABLE?

A meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee was held on April Stit when it was resolved that in future one meter be provided for each consumer of electricity for lighting purposes free of meter rent. In moving the adoption of the minutes, the Mayost said it was intended that customers should pay for all additional meters after the first. That concession would save the consumers 3s. to ss. per quarter. The com- mittee were doing all they possibly could for consumers, but they were obliged to put the works on a solid foundation. In support of this the MA.1,011 read out a list of some ; towns of greater magnitude than Warrington, where the prices charged for electricity were in excess of those charged in ‘Varrington, and where the electricity depart- ment was run at a loss, Brighton's deficiency being 210,000. Alderman BOLTON described the plant at several of the places mentioned as out-of-date. In conclusion, the Ma.von said the users of electricity for lighting purposes thought they ought to have the ; benefit of the £2,000 profit made iast year. The rate- payers, however, were the people who guaranteed to make up the loss when there was one, and they ought to have the benefit, which was 21. in the £ off the rates. Councillor WILKINSON seconded. Alderman BOLTON said the concession in the meter- rent was a trifle, but it would be appreciated. Still ho did not think the electric light users were getting enough. They paid Gd. per unit—with discount off. Id. or .41—and the Corporation were making 350 to 400 per cent. profit. The committee sold the same electricity for manufacturing purposes at something under 21. and were doing all they possibly could for the manufacturer. He did not see why the nears of electric light should pay double ; it was not far. The committee had put the matter on a false basis. It would appear that the whole of the profit was coming out of the users of electric light and the manufacturers got I the electricity at cost price. He did not think electricity ought to cost twice as much as gas. Councillor LORD agreed with Alderman Bolton that there was sadly too ranch difference in the charges for light and power and hoped the committee would make a substantial reduction to users for lighting purposes..„ _

„ Councillor CHANTLER expressed the opinion that the Gas Committee ought to take off the meter rent also. Councillor HAWTHORN said the prices were fully considered by the committee when they met a deputa- tion of the Tradesmen's Association a few months ago, and they felt that it was necessary in a new under- taking like that to build up a substantial reserve before they reduced the price, while it was hardly likely they I would reduce it when the price of coal and other material used in the department was going up. The committee was doing well, but he did not think it opportune to make a reduction. The charges for light- ing were not high compared with other towns—in fact he thought that the consumers for power purposes had more cause for complaint on that score. Councillor WILKINSON thought that if shopkeepers took everything into consideration—the lighting of their windows and the cleanliness of their goods, &c.— they would find electricity would compare favourably with gas. Alderman PIERPOINT, chairman of the Gas Com- mittee, denied that electric light was any better than gas. It was considerably dearer, and only half as good, and he thought he could claim that the gas of Warring- ton was admirable in every respect. (Laughter.) To those who had taken out their gas fittings and put in those ;or electric light, and who were not satisfiel with electric light and the charges, he would say "Send word to Mersey-street, and we shall be glad to re-instal the gas light which has served you well for many years.” (Laughter.) The Al A Yon. mentioned that the Tramways Committee paid lid. per unit for electricity, and their account amounted to £3,813. Who should complain? He thought the tramways. Alderman Bolton had only begun to complain since he had electric light installed in his house. (Laughter.) Alderman Bourox : If I find lam robbed I ought to tell somebody else. (Laughter.) The minutes were adopted. THE IRREGULARITIES IN THE SURVEYOR'S
DEPARTMENT.
SUGGESTED PROFESSIONAL AUDITOR.

The Borongh Treasurer submitted a report to the Finance Committee arising out of the irregularities in the Borough Surveyor's Department, with suggestions for an edit department. The report was referred to the General Purposes Committee.

When the minutes of the General Purposes' Committee came up for confirrnation,Aldermam PIEP.oiNT said this unfortunate question had been considered by a joint committee, aud the paragraph three in the Brierley report read: "This joint committee are of opinion that the time has arrived for the appointment of a pro- fessional auditor to audit the whole of the departments of the Corporation, and they recommend the General Purposes Committee to consider the advisability of making such appointment." He was sorry the mover or seconder did not explain what they had in their minds when that resolution was passed, because, taking the report, he pressed very strongly for the necessity of an internal auditor. He (Alderman Pierpoint) agreed that an audit of every account should be made, but it seemed to hira that Mr. Fairhurst wished someone in his °lnce, under his management and care, should audit the accounts. That was all right so far as it went, but he (Alderman Pierpoint) wanted not only the committee's accounts audited, but Mr. Fairhurst's accounts audited. (Hear, hear.) He did not want to do anything except point out the desirability of an inde- pendent auditor, and now the iron was hot he hoped the Finance Committee would press the matter forward. They wanted an audit department under its own responsibility, not under the responsibility of Mr. Fairhurst or anyone else. The question would come whether it would not be better after all to get an out- side responsible auditor—a chartered accountant—and divide up tho work between chartered accountants of the town in any way the committee might think best. He did not want to take any step that would further the appointment of an audit department except upon the lines he had mentioned. Alderman FORSIIINV : That was the intention of the joint committee. _

Alderman PiEnrorsrr : Very well, I have no more to say. The Tows CLERK Said the question would come up for consideration at the next meeting of the General Purposes Committee. The minutes were passed.

The debate on the THE VINDICATION Licensing Bill for England OF THE and Wales was brought to LICENSING BILL, a close on Monday, when the second reading stage was carried by 391 votes against 148—a majority of 246 for the Government. A small group of Liberals, several of whom are directly intere3ted in the licensed trade, voted against the Bill, and a larger number abstained from voting, but on the other hand several Unionist members voted in the majority. With the exception of two or three speeches the debate was maintained at a high level and was in marked contrast to the vituperation with which the Bill has been assailed in the con- stituencies. It has been a favourite allega- tion out of the House that a reduction in the number of licences would not mean a diminution of intemperance, but the principal speakers on the Opposition side refrained from taking up a position directly at variance with the reports Pf successive Commissions, and also with the claim made for the Act of 1901. Mr. Balfour repeatedly commended that measure to Parliament on the express ground that when licensing benches were able to award compensation they would feel free to reduce the number of licences. And for this reason he contended that the Bill deserved to be recognised as a measure of temperance reform. And yet when the present Government introduce a Bill to accelerate the process of reduction the country is told that there is no connection between the number of houses and excessive drinking ! It is, of course, beyond dispute that in dealing with the statistics of ietemperance the proportion of houses is not the only factor to be taken into consideration, for as is shown in the report of the Royal Commission, there is a higher average of intemperance where there is greater density of population. In short the conditions of crowded town life conduce to excessive drinking, but on the other hand there is a concurrence of testimony that facilities for drinking are a secondary factor in influencing the habits of the people. But the debate was mainly devoted to the pro- posed time limit of fourteen years, and on this the most contrary opinions were expressed, both con- cerning the nature of the monopoly value and the means by which it is proposed to extinguish it, In the United States and the Colonies licences are extinguished, when it is deemed expedient in the public interest, without compensation or a time limit, and the same rule obtained in this country up to 1901, and is still acted on in Scotland. But • the Government admit in their Bill that there is such a thing as monopoly value, based upon the expectation of renewal, and the Prime Minister defines it as the capitalised sum of the difference between the annual value of a licensed house and the rent which it would bring in if no licence were attached. Unfortunately, however, this reason- able view of what constitutes equitable compensation does not square with the tied-house system. For the brewers set up another standard of compensation altogether, and argue that in addition to the difference in the value of the house, the loss of profits by the firm of owners which supplies the liquor must be taken into consideration. Needless to say the Govern- ment refuse to recognise a claim which could not arise in the case of a free house, and is obviously inequitable where a firm of brewers has made a purely speculative investment for the sake of increasing its trade. So far as the length of the time limit is concerned, the principle laid down by the PRIME MiNucreu is that the period should be "as long end not longer than the time which would suffice for a prudent trader to make adequate provisions against the disappearance at the close of the time limit of that part of his profits which is to be attributed to the monopoly value of his licence." This statement on the part of the Government naturally opened the door to a good deal of discussion as to whether the term of four- teen years was a reasonable one, but several of the objectors to the Bill and particularly those who spoke for the licensed trade, contended that it would be just as much confiscation to extinguish the monopoly value in licences as it would be to take possession of a man's houses or land at the end of a term of years. This position was riddled

with argumentative shot and shell from the Liberal aide of the House, the obvious reply being given that there was no legal right to compensation at all, the time limit being a concession to the plea for equitable consideration. As to the losses alleged to be threatened by the Government Bill the speech of Mr. T. P. Wmeraxen was the most crushing reply to the gross exaggerations which have been indulged in. He produced figures showing that the chief fall in the value of brewery stock had taken place in the days of the late Government, and that there had been practically no fall in the value of brewery stocks on the Stock Exchange as a result of the introdaction of the Bill. But while some of the brewery companies iwhich had speculated rashly in tied houses had sustained heavy losses,a number of firms were in a strong financial position and perfectly able by the end of the time limit to wipe out the licence value. Sir T. P. WHITTAKER'S speech was practically an unanswerable one and we are glad to know that the facts and figures which he adduced are to be published broadcast as a reply to the terminological inexactitudes of the liquor interest. A good deal was said during the debate on the question of clubs, and it may be frankly admitted that from the standpoint of temperance reform the proposals of the Government are not as thorough• going as could be wished. But on the other hand it will not be denied that as far as they go they are in the right direction. And it may be reason- ably contended on behalf of the Government that they could not afford to over-weight the Bill. Both sides being the judges, it is as it stands the most comprehensive licensing measure which has yet been introduced into Parliament, and there is much to be said for the view that it would have been inexpedient to propose in the same Bill drastic legislation concerning clubs, for, after all, Governments, as well as individuals, have to consider what is possible as well as what is desirable. And it must not be forgotten that many of those who now attack the Government for not dealing drastically enough with clubs would in a different event have assailed them for interfering with the freedom of the British working man. We agree with temperance reformers generally in recognising that further legislation on this phase of the question will be necessary, but see no reason to dissent from the opinion of most of the Parliamentary supporters of the Government that in the present Bill they have gone as far as was prudent. While on this point it may be useful to correct the popular exaggeration concerning the increase in the number of clubs. It has been repeatedly said during the present discussion that for every suppressed licence a club is set up. So far from this being true the increase of clubs since the passing of Mr. Balfour's Act has been 558 as compared with a reduction of 3,934 on licences. This is an increase of one club for every seven sup- pressed licences, and even this statement requires qualification, for many of the new clubs which have been opened owe their existence not to a reduction in the number of licences, but to the growing tendency in the larger centres of popula- tion to establish political, sporting, and social clubs. This tendency has to be reckoned witb,and it will certainly become necessary in the near future for Parliarneut to consider whether the sale of alcohol in such institutions should not be sub- ject to the same excise duties and the same legal restrictions as ordinary licensed houses. In the meantime the Government is dealing with the greater problem of our licensing system, and, as Mr. Luovn-Gxouen reminded the House of Commons, the question at issue is not one of property merely, but of national well-being. The 200,000 convictions per year are only a fraction of the intemperance which exists, and worst of all there is a steady increase in female drinking. No Government which has set before itself the ideal of social reform and progress can afford to neglect this great hindrance to every forward movern out and it is matter for unqualified satisfaction that the House of Commons has endorsed the Govern- ment Bill by such triumphant majorities.

Sound finance—always a THE BUDGET. characteristic of Liberal Governments—and social reform, are the keynotes of the splendid Budget introduced by the new Premier,and late Chancellor, Mr. Asormar. "Old-age pensons at last " would be the exclamation of the majority when the text of the Budget proposals was made known, for Mr. ASQUITH has handsomely redeemed his promise to the poor by granting pensions of ss. per week to all people over 70 years of age and not possessed of an income exceeding 10s. per week. The pensions will come into actual being on January Ist next,and will doubtless be hailed as a very good beginning, by the aged poor. 'Tis true 65 years would he a better aga limit, but even Radical governments cannot reach perfection in one stride. Even they are bound by human limitations and must cut their coat according to the cloth. Mr. Alwyn' assures the country of this particular pension without inflicting any additional taxation to meet it. Better things may be hoped for in the future—at any rate so long as this wonderfully industrious, progressive and determined Govern- ment is in power. Mr. Lagurra was also able to announce that no new taxes whatever would be im- posed this year, and that,on the contrary, taxation would be remitted to the extent of nearly three and a half millions, This remission takes the form of a -reduction in the sugar duty by rather more than a half. The direct taxpayers had their turn in substantial relief last year ; it was now the turn of indirect taxation. Here sugar had clearly the best claim. For at one and the same time it is a burden on the raw materials of important industries, and it enhances the price of one of the prime necessaries of life. The same Budget state- ment is made additionally memorable by a record in the reduction of the National debt "unequalled in the history of British finance for 70 years." Had it no other interest, Mr. AsQuirn's Budget speech would (says the " Manchester Guardian ") be memorable for its proofs of the magnificent productiveness of Free Trade finance. Remember what the two Protectionist model countries, the two stock Edens, the patterns for a British El Dorado, are now doing. The United States are ruefully considering a year's deficit of £11,000,000. Germany has for some years had an annual deficit of some £13,000,000, and the prospective :increase of her National Debt during the next five years is estimated—by a sanguine Government—at £50,000,000. These are the kindly fruits of Protection. England meanwhile is paying off her National Debt even faster than these envied nations increase theirs. In the financial year just ended our total debt was reduced by nearly £17,000,000. By the end of thei financial :year now beginning it will have been :

reduced by another £15,000,000. Under the arrange- ments which our EXCHEQUER has been able to make, a debt which stood at £743,200,000 in March, 1006, will stand at £696,500,000 at this time next year. While Protectionist Germany hopes,with improved luck,to incur only £50,000,000 more of debt in five years, Free Trade England pays off nearly £50,000,000 of debt within three years. While Germany increases her annual tribute to hir creditors by about half a million in the year, England diminishes hers by nearly the same sum. This is what is called by Protectionist orators the bankruptcy of Ft ee Trade. The German and American arrangement is called scientific finance.

In the course of an Mrs. A. H. CROSF/ELD, interesting review of M.P. AND THE recent legislative progress LICENSING BILL, in the House of Commons, Mr. Crosfield deals at some length and quite emphatically with the Licensing Bill. The text of Mr. Crosfield's letter will be found in another column. We are sure the bulk of the townspeople will, together with our- selves, be delighted that Mr. Crostiehil has at last made public his views on the question of the day. There was never any doubt in well-informed quarters that the Borough Member would give whole-hearted support to such a reforming measure as the Licensing Bill, though there have , been people ready to suggest—and the wish was doubtless father to the suggestion—that Mr. Crosfield was not sound on the Licensing question. The tone of his letter, and the fact chat he voted for the second reading of the Bill, should dispel any such chimerical notions. Mr. Crosfieid is not a teetotaller, but he is in complete accord with the Liberal policy on Licensing reform. He strongly supports the reduction in the number of licences as likely to lesson the evils and abuses of drink and combats the idea that the Bill will cause any appreciable displacement of employ- ment, quoting the opinion of level-headed Labour leaders like Messrs. H.Vivian, Harvey, Shackleton and Henderson on the point. Mr. Crosfield lucidly expounds what he considers to be best in the Bill, and gives his opinion that as the complicated issue becomes more and more thoroughly understood, the weight of public opinion will run strongly for the Bill. We might add that it is running strongly already, even in Warrington, and the prospects of so great a measure becoming law could hardly be brighter. The Town Council on Toes- THE TOWN day did not provide a very Couleur,. thrilling entertainment for lookers-on. In fact the standard of interest in the proceedings was con- siderably below par, the subjects of discussion being decidedly of a humdrum character. True, there was some discussion on what one respected member always calls " tuberculerosis," but even this elicited nothing more striking than a declara- tion from Councillor Singleton that there is more disease caused through milk than beef. We can understand Mr. Singleton's point of view. He is more interested in beef than in mile, but his asser- tion lacks proof. Milk is said to be a "perfect food," and we have no doubt that purveyors of the lacteal fluid could make out a strong case in its behalf against any claim to superiority on the part of beef. The same Councillor complained of the delay in completing the paving at the top of Bridge-street, and asked for an explanation. We had some sympathy with Councillor Singleton on this point. Alderman Tinnion's explanation con- sisted mainly of a denial that there had been any delay, and there the matter ended. But the ,1 tradesmen and hahituis of Bridge-street will not be satisfied with the explanation. Possibly there , is some misunderstanding of the meaning of the ' word "delay." Evidently to Councillor Singleton it means one thing, and to Alderman Tinnion another. We find that one of Webster's definitions 'of the word is "lingering inactivity." This seems to us to fit the case nicely. There has certainly I been delay of this kind in the paving of this short section of street. Now, however, the work is pro- ceeding with marked expedition. We hope the Paving and Sewerage Committee will entirely redeem its character when it tackles the east side of the street. A smart performance in May might I tempt people to forget the "lingering inactivity of April.

Tradesmen do not seem to get much encourage- ment in their efforts to obtain cheaper electricity. The Electricity Committee is strongly averse to any reduction in the charge for current, and the bulk of the opinion of the Council is on their side. As a matter of fact the charge for lighting is not high when compared with the charges in other towns and the comparison between the prices per unit for lighting and for power is not a fair one. Councillor Wilkinson made use of a 'good argu- ment when he pointed out that the power users kept the station going during the day.time and thus cheapened the cost of running plant which would probably have to be " eating its head off" half the time if it were con- fined to supplying the demands of the electric light customers. The fact has also been considered that some of the largest power users could make their own electricity as cheaply as the Corporation and would at once do so if the cost of current became too high. Electric light is certainly dearer than gas, but it has advantages over the older illuminant that equal a considerable saving in actual cash to large shopkeepers. We can only counsel them to be patient. When the committee 11 has built up a substantial reserve fund there may be reasonable hope of concessions. At present it should be remembered that the Electricity and Tramways Department has contributed £2,000 to the relief of the current year's rates, and in this direction the shopkeepers will reap a substantial advantage which might reasonably be set against the cost of electricity.

There was much cause for Tun BAND OF encouragement in the War- Horz FESTIVAL. rington Band of Hope Festival which proved such a great attraction-at the Parr Hall on Wednesdiy and Thursday evenings. If local interest in temperance work amongst the rising generation may be gauged by the size of the audiences, then the cause is indeed flourishing. It was good to see the large hall crowded and the people following with evident delight the pretty ceremonial attendant upon the crowning of the Temperance Queen. The high place which the festival has won for itself amongst local entertainments speaks volumes for the devotion of the workers. The children knew their parts well and they com- ported themselves with that confidence and lack of self-consciousness which adds so much to the pleasure of children's performances. A prettier spectacle has probably never been seen on the Parr Hall platform—it was so full of colour and animation and the children found quite as much enjoyment in it as the spectators. The Band of Hope movement is doing a splendid work in Warrington and the profits accruing from the festival will provide the sinews of war for, it is hoped, even more effective propaganda. A very great deal remains to be done, but the outlook is brighter than it has been for a long time, and there is no better way of furthering the cause than by bringing up the children as faithful adherents. May the Warrington Band of Hope Union prosper increasingly in the coming year
