div.head: POLITICS OF THE WEEK.
div.p: THE POLITICS OF THE WEEK.

[FIIOII OUR LONDON CORRESPONDENT.] Politics are in full swing again, inside Parliament as well as out of it. Outside, at the by-elections, if there is a Unionist victory or a reduction of a Liberal majority, the rival claims for the credit are bewilder- i]g or amusing, according to one's mood. The Publican, tied or free, the Suffragette with or without her bell, the Tariff Ileformer with all the ardour of a Crusader, the Catholic Educationalist, the Irish Nationalist, and the Socialist (though the last-named was so badly out of it in North-West Manchester) are all ready to say:, "Alone I did it." But about Parlia- mentary majorities there is no mistake, and especially could there be no mistake about Monday night's division in the House of Commons. A GOOD THUMPING MAJORITY.

- - - -- - It was a good thumping majority that was given to the new Prime Minister at the end of the first debate in that House since he formed his Ministry —the debate on the Second Reading of the Licensing Bill. There was a famous leader of the House of Commons who had a trick of writing the numbers at such times on a piece of paper, which he carefully rolled up, and stowed away in a deep pocket. Mr. Asquith was con- tent to take a mental note of the numbers on Monday night ; they were easy and pleasant to remember. Por an amendment denouncing the Bill for sins of omission and commission —failure to promote temperance, violation of the principles of equity, 117 ; against this amendment, 337 —a neat and substantial, nicely rounded majority of 230. For the Second Reading of the Bill, 301 ; against it, 148—majority 240. It was a happy start for a new Prime Minister, and Mr. Asquith made no attempt to conceal his satisfaction. Neither have his more chivalrous Opponents said anything to detract from his victory. The comments made by the London "Globe " on Tuesday are worth a little notice for their bearing on the Wolverhampton Election. - - -

EAST WOLVERHAMPTON ELECTION. "The melancholy fact," says the "Globe," "that on a stand-or-fall division we can only muster 148 men into the lobby should have a steadying effect on those Who are being carried off their feet over the bye- elections." In the same article the " Globe," antici- pating the possibility of Mr. Amery's victory at Wolverhampton, furnished the Liberals with one reply in advance to the assumption since so freely made, that the "moral victory ' the victory not attained 'would, if attained, have been a victory for Tariff Reform. For it said, "Should it be his (i.e., Mr. Amery's) good fortune to achieve what would be the most striking victory in the whole campaign, woit may rest assured that resentment against this most unjust and confiscatory Bill will have played a large part in directing the issues of the ballot." Anotlier evening Paper on Tuesday—the "Westminster Gazette -- pointed out the important part played by the Catholic voters in the election. There are some eleven hun- dred of them—a substantial proportion of the electo- rate—and the Roman Catholic Bishop of Birmingham assured the Unionist candidate that he expected these voters would be solid for him. But it was not as Tariff Reformers that they were to vote solid for Mr. Amery. It was as opponents of the Government on the religious education question. In the circumstances Mr. Thorne did well to save the seat. He will be a credit to his party in the House. He is an orator as Well as a good party politician. THE LICENSING BILL.

Returning to the debate oa the Licensing Bill, it is probably fair to say that it saved Mr. Thorne from defeat. The new member complains that he had to struggle against want of knowledge. This is quite a charitable way of putting it ; since he had to fight also against positive error and misconception as to the meaning and scope of the Licensing Bill. The se9ond reading debate must have cleared much of this away. But, unfortunately, the finest speech in the debate that made by the Prime Minister himself —was not made until late on the eve of the poll. The whole controversy of the Licensing Bill turns on the question whether we are going to be unjust to the brewer and the publican in order to stop the evils of intemperance—in other words whether the Bill is fair to the trade. If it is not, a man's beer of course will cost him more. But apart from the fact that there are plenty of people nowadays who are either. not beer-drinkers at all, or who do not mind paying a fair price for good beer, the main point is : Is the Bill cricket ? Is it fair ? Is it straight ? It is wonderful how many voters will suffer themselves through the rates or taxes (for that is what it means in the long all 1). rather than let it be said that we hit any class i 101;0 our legislation. The clear and decisive way n walch the Prime Minister get to the bottom of this question, aided by his colleagues' speeches in the "arse of the debate, which left him free to deal with ,one or two essential points, will make all future I)Y:electlons easier for the Ministerial candidates, in spite of the exertions of the Trade. Indeed, it is by 00 means certain that the Trade will be quite as enthusiastic electioneerers in future ; for the net result of the debate is to make a publican pause and ask whether he is wise to fight so hard against the Bill.
A GLIMPSE AT AN ALTERNATIVE.

. - This is how Ifr. Asquith put it. The alternative is between the Bill and high licence duties. It is not a question of the trade being robbed. It is a question whether they are to go on for ever making a good thing out of the trade monopoly the public gives them, while the public can neither share the profits which g; partly create, nor control their own property in monopoly. If the Chancellor of the Exchequer "one to raise the beer duty, or to claim a higher licence duty, would that be confiscation, or would it be 'ithin his right in the public behalf? Not a member could say that this would be confiscation. In fact some of the opposition frankly and fairly said "No." Whereupon Mr. Asquith asked how it could be confisca- tion to arrange that the Trade should retain their Illonepoly value for fourteen or fifteen years, before the Public claimed their right of control again. The deep Silence that greeted this triumphant argument l'oggested that the Opposition were reflecting whether at would not be better after all to take the Bill and fight shy of the high licence duties thus suggested by the Prime Minister to his Chancellor of the Exchequer "—Mr. Lloyd-G eorge.

div.head: TWO NEW PEERS.
div.p: THE TWO NEW PEERS.

- - - - .„„.Viseount Morley of Blackburn and Viscount wolverhampton of Wolverhampton, did not seem to be sPending a happy quarter of an hour on Tuesday çevening, when, under the tutelage of the Duke of orfolk, Earl Marshal, and Garter King of Arms, they went through what is commonly called the Picturesque ceremonial of introduction to the House of Lords. Imagine Mr. John Morley and Sir Henry ?owler, weighted with scarlet and ermine robes, and heavy black cocked hats, with their sponsors and the officials already named, making separate processions through that house, kneeling to their old fellow- Radical on the Woolsack to present their patents, then marching round the Chamber and making obeisances at Riven points and times. It was noticed that Lord Morley most innocently neglected some of these, and was more quick to take note of amused friends at the bar of the House than to absorb himself in ceremonial recognition of the empty Throne, or the gilded mace, until he came to the Viscount's bench. Even here, when being apparently directly coached by Garter King of Arms in the solemn business of taking off the cocked hat three times to salute the now far-off Lord Chancellor, it was Positively delightful to witness the inaptitude of this brilliant peer and holder of the Oraer of Merit at learning his latest lesson—a lesson in superfluous salutations. He afterwards had the courage to come a.„11(1 himself act as one of the sponsors to Sir Henry owler, now Lord Wolverhampton, Lord Althorp "bag the other. But with regard to all this antiquated ceremonial it would not surprise us if his inmost thought took the form of one of his old and most anted political mots, "Let us mend it or end it." Afterwards, both the new peers looked much happier In their places on the front Ministerial bench divested ' of their heavy scarlet and ermine. LORD CREWE'S DEBUT. Their first experience on this bench was to watch the dlibut of Lord Crewe as leader, and to hear his enlogy of the late Prime Minister. Lord Crewe die- charged this duty with his customary grace,beginning rst With a tribute to his predecessor in the leader- Lordl Ripon, which enabled him to introduce ;Oaself modestly in his new capacity, and bespeak the elof the House. Lord Lansdowne responded Chivalrously to this appeal, assured Lord Crewe that be had already Fained the House's admiration of his tactful and considerate leadership, and commented on Pansgyrie of the late Prime Minister in a respon- " PASSING IT ON, ,o,,i'lt_;Bt ono little story with a Tariff Reform moral to up " Politics of the week." A well-known ewer Wan before the Hop Industry Committee the

? other day—Mr. Graham Aldous. He was friendly to the hop-growers, but at the same time informed the • Committee that a certain quantity of foreign hops were necessary to his trade not for cheapness, but for flavour. If an imp-wt duty on foreign hops sere put on, there must b• a corresponding relief to the ; brewers if the result was an increase in the price of ! hops. Said Mr. Rowlands, a member of the Committee, 1" You want to pass the duty on to the public ?" "Wo ! don't want to pay it," said Mr. Aldous. Every time you come to a concrete case of tariff reform, it breaks down. It is a tax, not co the foreigner, but on the ! home consumer in the end. Our hops will cost Us i more !

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.

Result of East Wolverhampton ele:nion :—Thorne won by one odd trick in hearts ! Thank goodness, Amery couldn't " double." * * There was a Council meeting on Tuesday, but not a single nice plump Alderman offered to accept our thallengs to cycle over Warrington Bridge, taking the tramway track on the east side. If the holes get much worse someone will be going through into the river.

* * * Mr. Winston S. Churchill will,we expect,be returned as member for Dundee to-day. Manchester's loss will in that case, be the Scottish city's gain. It is a mis- fortune for Lancashire that the President of the Board of Trade is likely to represent a constituency so remote from the County Palatine. * * * Arising out of the lamentable Briarley case we are likely to have an audit department under the Cor- poration, and a professional auditor or auditors for the whole of the Borough accounts. The matter will come up for discussion by the General Purposes Com- mittee, which consists of the whole Council,on Monday

* * * Apropos of the Grand Duke Michael as an author, it may be noted that the Couutess Torby is the grand- daughter of a great Russian man of letters, the poet and patriot Poushkine, whose daughter married morganatically a brother of a Grand Duke of Luxem- bourg and was the mother of the Countess Sophia of Merenburg, now wife of the Grand Duke. * * * When Mr. Gooch was recently elected for Peckham we were told that it was really very unfair to him (a tota labstainer, too) to say that he owed his election to the Trade. We notice, however, that at the Hotel Cecil last week Mr. Gooch was one of the speakers at the annual dinner of the Licensed Victuallers' Central Protection Society. After all, these alliances cannot very well be concealed, and people will think all the better of Mr. Gooch for thus nailing his colours to the Trade mast.

* * * Correspondents in the Newport Division speak very hopefully of Mr. Francis Neilson's chances and the splendid fight which he is making for Liberalism in that hitherto ultra-Conservative constituency is worthy of all admiration. At his public meetings he is having the support of Mr. R. L. Outhtvaite, we'l known to Warrington Liberals, and that redoubtable worker Mr. Joseph Howes, whom the " Liverpool Daily Post and Mercury" correspondent dacribes as one of the most popular of speakers. * * We suppose there can be no doubt that there is a suicidal tendency in some families. At any rate there is strong evidence to support the theory in the circum- stances indirectly connected with the suicide of Mr. H. Clare, a Warrington tradesman, on Thursday. It was stated at the inquest that the deceased's father and two of his brothers had also committed suicide, whilst he also made an attempt to hang himself at the age of 14. In the present instance, drink has once more been a contributory cause to the mental state of the deceased when he committed the tragic act. We wonder what the proportion of suicides traceable to drink is, as compared with those due to other causes? * * * There was a very interesting discussion on the opium question on Wednesday night in the House of Commons, and Colonel Seely, in his first speech as Colonial Under-Secretary, bad the great satisfaction of being able to announce that on Monday the Govern- ment telegraphed to the Governor of Hong Kong that the opium dens must be closed. The system is also speedily to be ended in Ceylon. Certainly we cannot afford to lag behind China in this matter; and we are glad to read Sir Edward Grey's speech, in which he recommended the Government so to act in India as to co-operate with China in getting rid of the curse of opium-eating. * * * . . . . .

With suffragists all around us, it is interesting to remember that in France a woman stood as a candi- date for Parliament as long ago as 1849. She was a Madame Desroches, and her election address—the essential passage in it, at all events—ran as follows : MEN ! What are you? TYRANTS? Or PHILOSOPHERS? Or FOOLS ?
As TYRANTS we \Till fight yon. As PHILOSOPHERS we will argue yea down

As FOOLS we express our contempt for you. It is sad to relate that, in spite of her brave words, Madame Desroches failed to receive what the Americans call a plurality. The power of doing a good action is happiness enough.— Carmen Ere who craves for drink will live to whine for bread.—ll. B. Sheridan. Old age appears hideous to us until we have to choose between it and death.—Diane. The man who does not think two heads better than one may be safely put down as a—father of twins. B. Sheridan. . _
A man's first care should be to avoid the reproaches of his own heart ; his next to escape tho censures of the world.—Addison. . . .
Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm. —Emerson.. - -

There's nothing but what's bearable, so long as a man can work. —George Eliot. We are really alive only when we find delight in the goodwill of others.—Go3the. Life is ton short to waste in critic peep or cynic bark, quarrel or reprimand ; 'twill soon be dark.— Emerson.

Here is an interesting illustration for land law reformers: Mr. James Hondas White, M.P., has obtained some interesting information with regard to the rating authority's valuation of a piece of land for rating purposes, and the landlord's valuation to the Admiralty for purchase. The ground is situated to the west of Greenock on the Clyde. It embraces 10 acres of land and 41 acres of foreshore. The Admiralty wished to use it for the erection of a torpedo factory, and purchased it for .£27,225. " rhe foreshore," says Mr. White, " was treated as of no value in the valua- tion Roll, and the 10 acres formed part of a property of 43 acres, which as a whole was entered on the Valuation Roll as of an annual value of 5.75." This is a record transaction of its kind, as the price works out to about 1756 years' purchase of the rate- able value ! We have been told a thousand times on platforms, in the press,in the House of Commons and the House of Lords that the value of such land cannot be ascertained. We are told that if the Government do fix the value of such land, they will inflict a terrible injustice on the landowner ; but we take it on our- selves toesay that in no case will they ever treat the landowner in the outrageous manner he treated them in the case."

_ * * * Mr. A. H. Crosaeld, M.P. paid a flying visit to Warrington last week-end and gave further evidence of his well-known interest in healthy sport by attend- ing the charity bowling match between Rylands' Bros. team and the rest of the Association at Gorsey-lane and the final of the Works Football Competition at Wilderspool. The Member, who was looking very well after his short sojourn in France, had a cordial reception on each ground, and at the close of the f•ootball match he delivered a short but happy speech n which he rightly congratulated the players upon the °condition" which enabled them to play at such a good pace on a summer-like afternoon. On Tuesday Mr. Crosfield was in Manchester and opened the Grocers' and Allied Trades Exhibition in the St. James's Hall—an event of great interest to those closely con- nected with the business in the Northern counties. His remarks were particularly well chosen and the confident hope which he expressed that commerce would act as peacemaker by bringing the democracies of different nations into closer relations and eventually abolish the brutal and disastrous arbitrament of war met with evident approval. Next Tuesday Mr. Crosfield is to open an exhibition of the works of the late George Sheffield, an artist with close local associations, at the Warrington Art Gallery, and on Saturday May 23rd he will, accompanied by Mrs. Crosfield, attend the Warrington Musical Festival at the Parr Hall. SIIGAR, IS MUCH DEARER,-.-Advt.

div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, May 9, 1908.

Theft of Timber. Joseph Harrop, labourer, Crossley-street, pleaded guilty at Warrington Borough Court on Thursday, to a charge of stealing three pieces of timber, of the value of 3s. 4d., from the shipping depot of R. A. Naylor, Limited, and was fined 20s. and costs or one month's imprisonment. The Scene at an Inquest At the Warrington Occasional Court on Saturday, before Colonel ifuckton, Richard Sharp, farmer, of Dam-lane, Rixton, was charged with having been drunk the previous night. This was the sequel to the scene at the inquest held by Coroner Brighouse at Glazebrook Station on the victims of the train tragedy. Sharp, who was one of the jurymen, was exceedingly talkative, and es entually Mr, Brighouse asked the police to take him into custody for being drunk.— Sharp was fined 2s. 6d. SUGAR IS MUCH DEARER.—Advt. Sequel to a Stockton Heath Burglary. At the quarterly meeting of the Cheshire Standing Joint Committee, at Chester Castle, on Saturday, a claim was received from the Warrington Infirmary Authorities for £l2 Os., in respectro the maintenance of William Peel, during his detention in the Infirmary from the 23rd January to the 13th April, 1903, he having been apprehended on charges of burglary and housebreaking.—The Chief Constable (Colonel Hamersley) said the man was in the Infirmary 82 days and the authorities asked for 3s. per day for his main- tenance, which seemed to him a very moderate sum. Ile recommended that the accounts be paid.—lt was resolved that the claim be paid. Premier in name, Premier in quality. PREMIER CYCLES from 6 guineas.—J. S. UARLAND, 51 to 55 Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Better in Gaol than out. At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, before M. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, Mr. R. T. Fairclough and Councillor Stott, James Wood, of no settled address,pleadecl guilty to loitering in Bridge-street with intent to commit a felony, at 12.20 that morning.—Sergeant Barnett said he was in company with P.C. Hewitt in Bridge-street, when lie saw prisoner loitering about in a suspicious manner. Witness went to him, and he said he had only come out of gaol that morning and wanted to break in somewhere. He said if he could not get in any other way, he would put his foot through a plate glass window.—The Chief Constable said prisoner had been convicted several times for felony. He told the Sergeant be was better in gaol than out.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month. SUGAR IS DEARER.—Advt. " Not English Fair Play." At the Borough Police Court on Saturday, Samuel Allen, a bricklayer, of no settled address, appeared on remand from Thursday, charged with drunkenness an doing wilful damage.—The Chief Constable said that having regard to the way in which prisoner con- ducted himself in the dock on Thursday, the Bench thought it was desirable that he should be examined by a doctor. He had been examined by two doctors, and the doctors would be well advised if they sent him to the Union for 14 days as a pauper lunatic, and if necessary he could thee be conveyed to an asylum. He had recently been an inmate of Winwick Asylum. —Prisoner : lam as sane as any man. Don't send me there ; it is not fair to send ma away as a lunatic all tha days of my life.—The Beech ordered prisoaer's removal to the Workhouse for 11 days.—Prisaner : That is not English fair play. Six GUINEAS will purchase a fully guaranteed PREMIER CYCLE. Inspection invited.—J. S. GA.R. AND, 51,53, & 55 Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Unbidden Guests. A case of housebreaking of a particularly audacious type took place on Saturday night Mr. W. Price, an Inland Revenue official who resides at Paddington, had ,been entertaining same friencia to dinner and later in the evening, to some music. As he was bidding them "good-bye " he noticed a ladder lying on the lawn, which caused him to make a search. Ire then discovered that burglars had obtained the ladder and placed it to one of the bedroom windows, by which they entered and appropriated a number of gold watches, rings and other jewellery. They got clear away and nothing further bad been heard of them. 'Another case of housebreaking occurred a few days ag in Henry-street. In the absence of the occupants the door was forced open with a jemmy and several things are missing. AsHiev's, New Address 4, Butterraarket Street.—Advt Local Exhibitors at the Royal Academy. Warrington is this year again well represented at the Royal Academy. Mr. Henry Woods has two pictures, "In Friuli: The Knitters " and "Campo S. Maria della Salute," the first being two girls seated at the base of some steps from an old doorway, and the second a simple and charming study of sunlight and shade. Sir Luke Fildes has two portraits, Lady Royds and Mrs. Henry Blyth, and a :picture in his former style of a Venetian flower girl "4„0 Giardiniera." Mr. Oswald Garside has two large water colours "High upon the sea" a picture of solitude, sand dunes and sky, and " Lowlands " a scene at Bosham in -Sussex. Mr. Wilmot Lunt has a small drawing in Tempera colour entitled "The World Forgetting," a picture of two lovers walking along an avenue. Miss Ethel Mottram, a new exhibitor, has two etchings in the Black and White Room, "Lamb Building—The Temple" and "Fig Tree Court—The Temple." Messrs. W. and S. Owen exhibit an architectural drawing of Memoiial Screen, St. Elphin's Warrington. Mr. Oswald Garside has also a water colour at the Paris Salon, entitled "A Stranger in a Strange Land," representing an Italian minstrel girl at a doorway. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—IINDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LaNclsnin.E.—Advt. Fatal Fall From a Ladder. On Tuesday evening Mr. Brighouse conducted the adjourned inquest at the Police Station touching the death of Water Coleman, labourer, 6, Back Stamford- street, who died as the result of injuries received on Tuesday morning week by falling from a ladder at the Mersey Lead Works the previous day. Mr. Steel appeared for the relatives, and Mr. IV. Sloane (manager) and Mr. P. J. Frith (secretary) represerted the Mersey White Lead Co. Mr. Sumner, factory inspector, was also present.—The evidence showed that Coleman, along with five other men, was engaged in carrying boxes of lead from a waggon on the ground to a stack room above. Coleman was carrying a box of lead weighing 851 b. on his head up the ladder when the box fell. He then fell backwards and his head came in contact with the ground, and he, unfor- tunately, died from his injuries the following morning. —Joseph Henry Skelhorn, labourer at the works, said carrying the lead in the manner described was his usual work.—Mr. Sloane gave evidence, and, in answer to Mr. Sumner, said Coleman had been employed at the works five weeks. In answer to Mr. Steel, witness said he had been manager at the works about 20 years , and this was only the second fatal accident which had ' occurred.—The Coroner said employers were anxious to get the work done in the most expeditious and safest manner possible, because it did not pay them to do otherwise nowadays. —The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death." £l4 Hs Good second-hand piano.—WOOD, London rd., Stockton Heath. Tunings and repairs,—Advt. Presentation to Mr. Monro. Mr. James Monro, who has retired from the position of manager of Dallam Brewery, was on Tuesday presented with a chased floral mounted silver salver, a silver two-bottle inkstand, and a silver cigar box, as a token of esteem and regard from the ernploy4s at the , brewery.—Mr. Ernest Parry, who made the presentation said they were assembled on rather an unpleasant duty. That was to say " Good bye " to Mr. Monro. As they all knew for some years he had not enjoyed the best of health, and by his doctor's orders he had retired from business. They sincerely hoped that by so doing he would soon be restored to (rood health and have a long life. By his kind, ' courteous, and straightforward manner he had so endeared himself to all of them that they would miss him very much.—Mr. Thomas Cox (superintendent of the cask department) also testified to Mr. Monro's popularity.—Mr. Monro, who was received with loud cheers and musical honours, said be had been 20 years in the employ of Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, and the time had passed all too quickly. Ten years out of those twenty he had been at Dallam-lane and those ten years had passed faster than any. He had seen many youths come, and many old ones go, and now the time came when he, too, must go to the rear and join the old brigade. If he had ever said a rude word or in any way acted cruelly, be asked them now to forgive and forget. He asked them all to do all they could for Messrs. Peter Walker and Son, and support, in the same way that they had supported him, his successor, Mr. Hutton. In getting Mr. Hutton they had secured the services of one of the best men in the brewing trade. He (Mr. Monro) was sorry to part with them, but his doctor said if he was to live many years, he must get change of air and change of scenery. He thanked them all on his own and Mrs. Monro's behalf for those excellent and valuable presents. (Loud applause.) SUGAR IS DEARER.—Advt.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL FESTIVAL
Splendid Entries.

The first Warrington Musical Festival to be held in the Parr Hall on Saturday, May 23rd, will be a red letter event and should appeal to all lovers of music in Warrington and district. Admirable arrangements have been made by a strong and representative com- mittee and there is every indication that complete success will crown their efforts. The entries have realized the highest expectations and upwards of 1,000 competitors will figure in the various contests. The Mayor (Alderman Sraethurat) is the President of the festival and he will preside over the afternoon pro- (feedings. Mr. A. H. Crosfield M.P. and Mrs. Crosfield have intimated their intention of attending the festival. Mr. Crosfield has presented a valuable shield for the chief choral competition (for mixed choirs) and the trophy will be handed over to the winning choir by Mrs. Crosfield. This competitioa will afford a rare musical treat, the following well- known choirs having entered : —Blackpool Orpheus, Southport, Earlestown Glee Society, Runcorn and Widnes Choral Socity, Stretford Glee and Madrigal Society, Salford Select Choir, Preston Vocal Union, St. Helens Mixed Choir. For the male voice cboir competition the entries included the famous Manchester Orpheus Choir. Another great attraction will be the 11 contest for church and chapel choirs, which is exciting great interest locally. The entries are : —Stockton Heath Wesleyan, Bewsey-road Wesleyan, Bold-street Wesleyan, and Leh-street Primitive Methodist. The trophy for this contest has been presented by Mr. James Dodds. The children's choral contest willbe a pleas- ing feature, the following choir S having entered : Warrington Band of Hope' Sutton United, Preston Council School, Warringtonßeamont Council School, and Rhyl-street Mission, Bootle. The committee have been fortunate in securing two such capable adjudi- cators as Dr. W. G. McNaught and Mr. Wilfred Jones, 11.A.11. The accompanists will be Mr. W. 11. Payton, Mus. Bac., and Mr. E. Wilkes. Through the good offices of Mr. E. Lloyd-Jones (chairman of the ifestival Committee), the audiences will have the ' pleasure of hearing, in addition to the competitions, solos by Miss Frances Andrews (contralto, of Queen's Hall, London) and violin solos by Miss A. Backsheen Wood who has on several previous occasions appeared with great success in Warrington. The plan of reserved seats in the centre gallery (3s. for the two, concerts), is open at Wadswcrths, Sankey-street. Tickets for other parts of the hall may be obtained from any member of the committee.

div.head: LOCAL TRADESMAWS SUICIDE. -- Found Hanging in an Outbuilding. -- Remarkable Family Record.
div.p: LOCAL TRADESMAWS SUICIDE. -- Found Hanging in an Outbuilding. -- Remarkable Family Record.

The circumstances attending the death of Henry Clare, a well-known horse breaker and bird dealer, Flag-lane, whose body was found hanging in an out- building at the rear of his premises on Thursday, were inquired into at the Police Station yesterday afternoon by Coroner Brighouse.—Mr. Browne represented the relatives of the deceased. Mrs. Mary Clare, wife of the deceased, said her husband was 47 years of age. He had been drinking heavily during the past six weeks and she had left hint several times owing to his drunken haliits. She recently left him but she returned home again on Saturday last. When she went away her husband generally engaged her niece but this time he engaged another housekeeper.ffer niece then went to live with her sister. On Wednesday she and her husband hada quarrel about the housekeeper. When they were quarrelling he got a knife and drew it across her throat, causing a scratch about three inches long. They went to bed, and at 6.15 the next morning her husband got up. He went downstairs to light the fire and at seven o'clock she herself got up and missing deceased went into the yard and found the gate was bolted. She tried to open the door of the outbuilding but it was fastened. She went for assistance, the door was forced open and there she saw her husband hanging. John Davies, an insurance agent, whose office is in Golborne-street, said that the deceased came to his lodgings on Wednesday night and witness went back with him to his house and stayed there some time. He was leaving him early the following morning when Clare said that witness was the last man he would shake hands with. Witness stayed a little longer and on going the deceased promised to go to bed and be a good man. I He did not see any marks on Mrs. Clare's neck. Mrs. Clare said that the deceased drew the knife across her throat after the previous witness left. When her husband was getting up he looked at her throat and said " Never mind." Davies continuing, said that when he left the deceased's house Mrs. Clare was very excited. The Coroner : She was jealous about the house- keeper ? Witness : There was nothing mentioned about the housekeeper while I was there. Arthur Hill, Golborne-street, said that about 7.30 on Thursday morning Mrs. Clare came to him and said she was afraid her husband had done something to himself. He went to the house and broke open the door of the outbuilding and found the deceased hanging from a beam in the roof of the outbuilding. The door had been fastened with a large wedge. He cut the man down and carried him into the house. He did his best to restore animation but his efforts were of no avail as the man was already dead. Mr. Browne said that the deceased's father and two brothers committed suicide. . .
A Juryman said that he remembered tho deceased attempting to hang himself when he was fourteen years of age. The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst temporarily insane."

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The World's Great Snare."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. " The World's Great Snare."

Those who like a play full of thrills will find some- thing to their taste at the theatre this week, where the attraction is Mr. W. Alexander-Dallas' American spectacular melodrama " The world's great snare." The play treats of exeiting life in the West, and there are such pleasant incidents as an explosion in a gold mine and a fight for life in "the celebrated black canyon" which are loudly acclaimed from the gallery. Chief honours go to Mr. David 0-. Noble who takes the unenviable part of Lascelle La Mort. a villain of the deepest dye, with fine power. Mr. Wilford Dew. hurst also does well as Royal Keno, scant to U.S. Army, whose hairbreadth escapes are a source of perpetual wonderment. Miss Jessie Elvin achieves considerable success as Wild Rose, the Queen of the plains. The staging of the play is all that could be desired.
NEXT WEEK'S BIG- ATTRA.CTION. "HIS HOUSE IN ORDER.".

" His House in Order" will be presented at the Warrington Theatre on Monday next for six nights only. The play was produced at the St. James' Theatre, London, in 1903, was given a tremendous reception, and received the most enthusiastic praise from the London Press that has been accorded to any modern play of late years. It ran for 427 consecutive performances to overflowing and delighted audi- ences, and the title has now become a household word throughout the length and breadth of the British Isles. The play is intensely human, possessing a strong and moving story, handled with such skill that the interest steadily increases till a very high pitch is reached in the third act, and yet the fourth (and last) does not simply bring the play to a close, but contains some of , its most powerful scenes.. We have many plays that excite, touch or amuse. " His House in Order" not only does all this, but appeals to the inmost feelings and one comes away moved and uplifted as by some strong personal experi- ence. We trust that the public of Warrington will take the opportunity of witnessing this great play which is being presented by a specially selected London Company approved by Mr. George Alexander. Mr. H. Ralph Kitupton, who is bringing this celebrated comedy to Warrington, is the youngest theatrical manager in the United Kingdom. He is not, however, without a great deal of experience. He has been with Mr. George Alexander at the 3t. James' rheatre for the last eight years, during which time Mr. Alexander produced some of his most successful productions, the biggest success of all undoubtedly being " His House in Order," for which play Mr.lKimpton was stage manager for the first production.

div.head: ROYAL THEATRE OF VARIETIES.
div.p: ROYAL THEATRE OF VARIETIES.

During the week Madame Annie Millwood, a con- tralto vocalist well-known to local concert-frequenters in the days of the old Public Hall, Rylands-street, has been singing nightly with conspicuous success:at the above-mentioned place of amusement. Warrington has nothing but kindly memories of Madame Hall- wood's capabalities as a public singer. Iler fine con- tralto voice still possesses the rich tones and pleasing flexibility that always characterised it and she yet successfully appeals to one's sympathies in songs of the standard of " The Lost Chord " with which she has entertained her audiences this week.
SUGAR IS MUCH DEAITHR.—AdVt.

div.head: LOCAL NEWS.
div.p: LOCAL NEWS.
Notice. Owing to pressure on our space this week we have bent reluctantly compelled to omit reports of the meetings of the Bands Association and Stockton Heath Parochial Committee.

SUGAR IS DEARER.—Advt. Musical Successes. At the recent Theoretical Examination of the Incorporated Society of Musicians, two pupils of Miss Roscollor, Lorne House School, were among the suc- cessful candidates,Dorothy Perdue obtaining 83 marks pass, and SJphie Clatworthy 91 marks honours. Stockton Heath Wesleyan Sunday School. The anniversary sermons in connection with the above will be preached to-morrow (Sunday), by the Rev. S. T. Bosward, of Rhyl. In the afternoon a cantata entitled " The flower mission " will be rendered. On Monday evening the Rev. S. T. Bosward will lecture on " Great talkers of our times."

div.head: A_ SUGAR IS MUCH 'DEAREIL—Advt.
div.p: A_ SUGAR IS MUCH 'DEAREIL—Advt.

Warrington Horse Parade. The eighth annual parade will take place on Satur- day nest and promises to be a great success. Entries which are to be made at 110, Bridge-street, close to-day (Saturday) at four o'clock. A special class has been provided for owners in the habit of working their own horses. A collection in ail of local charities will be made along the lino of route. The Late Alderman John Roberts. At St. Peter's Church on Sunday morning the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) unveiled a brass tablet which has been placed in St. Peter's Church to the memory of the late Alderman John Roberts who for many years rendered devoted service as a church- warden. The unveiling ceremony toDk place just prior to the sermon by the Vicar. Advancing te the pillar at the side of which the late Alderman sat for many years, the Mayor, with purple streamers, drew aside the white. cover bearing a purple cross (this having made by Mrs. Steel), saying : "To the glory of God and to the memory of the late Alderman John Roberts." -

ASHLEY'S, New Address 4, Buttermarket Street.— Adv Death of Mrs. A. Clara. We regret to announce the death of Mrs. Ann Clare, which took place in her sixty-third year, at her residence, Winwick-street, on Saturday night. The deceased lady had been suffering from bronchitis for twelve months, but only took to her bed a month ago. She had acted as sub-postmistress at the Winwick- street office for fourteen years, and her death will come as a great shock to her numerous friends. Much sympathy is felt with the widower and four children in their bereavement. The funeral took place on Tuesday at Hill Cliffe,theßev.J.F.Nfatthews officiating. The chief mourners were :—Messrs. James Clare (husband), Ralph and James Clare (sons), Thomas Tongue (son-in-law), James and Arthur Tongue (grandsons), James and William Beswiek (nephews A large number of floral tributes were sent and there was a large attendance at the graveside. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCIC FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Chancellor Espin's Mishap. Chancellor Espin should have attended at the War- Parish Church on Thursday, for his annual visitation for the admission of churchwardens and sidesmen. The various church officers had assembled, when the Rector of Warrington (Rev. Canon Willis) announced that he had received a telegram from Chancellor Espin to the effect that he had met with a slight accident during the night and was unable to be present, and expressing regret that he was unable to hold his visit- ation. The rector added that he was sure all those ' present would be sorry at the enforced absence of the Chancellor. The Rector, on behalf of the Chancellor, held the court, but no address was given.

SD OAR, IS 1.113C11 DEARER.—Advt. TRY GILLETTE SAFETY RAZORS for comfort in shaving.—Agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51-55, Bridge street, Warrington.—Advt. Misapplied Zeal for Gardening. At the Borough Police Court on Alonday two boys named William Green and John Joseph Leigh, both of Haydock-street, pleaded guilty to stealing eleven packets of garden`seeds. valued at 11d., from the stall of William Powell in the Market-place on Saturday night.—The Chief Constable said the wife of the pro- secutor saw Green take the seeds and she informed her husband. Green admitted stealing the seeds, and then made a statement implicating Leigh. Mr. Powell had lost 1,000 packets of seeds during the past few weeks.—Mr. Powell corroborated.—Leigh said they wanted the seeds to plant in the back yard.—The defendants were each ordered to receive four strokes with the birch-rod.

ASHLEY'S, New Address 4, Battermarket Street.—Advt Appleton Rifle Club. Saturday was the opening day of the club's shooting season. The weather was exceptionally .fine and warm, and a large number of members put in an appearance at the range. There were no entries for the National Rifle Associations' Certificate, those who were present preferring to confine themselves to practice, with a view to making their mark later on. The N.R.A. targets for this year proved rather puzzling to the members, as they alb entirely different from those previously used, being round instead of square and having what is technically known as an "invisible bull." In plain language this means that part of the " inner " as well as the bull, is black, the two parts being separated by a white line invisible to the firer There appears to be every prospect of the club having a successful season, and of its popularity being fully maintained.
SUOAR IS MUCH DEARER.--Advt. PUBLIC, BENEFIT-UNDER TDB CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—AdVt.

Girls' Club, Silver-street. The closing meeting of last winter's season was held on Monday evening when seventy-one of the girls who had made the best attendance partook of a substantial tea, which was evidently much enjoyed. After the meal a pleasant evening was spent, presided over by Miss B. Dutton, who congratulated the large number who had made excellent attendances, and who had shown snch good conduct and industry. She afterwards distributed the many garments neatly sewn and numerous pairs of stockings, the fruit of the season's work. The hon. secretary (Miss Ashdown) reported that the names of 101 members were on the books. Her name and that of the Matron (Mrs. Timmins) were received by the girls with great enthusiasm, and expressions of gratitude, as were also those of the members of the" 0" Temperance Society who greatly assist the work of the club every week. The girls sang several pieces, sacred and secular, and some solos with choruses were given. A dialogue and recitations also gave the audience much pleasure Oranges were distributed at the close, and it was announced that the club would be re-opened in October.

ASHLEY'S New, Address 4, Buttermarket Street .—Adv oddfellowship. On Satrday evening last at the Loyal Olive Branch Lodge L0.0.F.(M.U.) Warrington District,there was an interesting event in the form of a "Social" at which a presentation of a framed past officer's certificate to P.G. Andrew Hay (who has recently completed his term of office) was made. The Lodge room was filled to its utmost capacity, The meeting was presided over by N G.William Winstanley and the fact that the District Officers honoured the occasion with their presence lent an additional element of interest to the proceedings. The presentation was made on behalf of the Lodge by Prov. G. H. Lot Brooks who said that lie had always found P.G. Hay honest, straightfor ward, upright, con- scientious and faithful t the duties he had to perform , and he trusted he would act up to those noble prin- ciples as faithfully in the future as he had done in the past. (Applause.) Deputy G.M. Fred Freeman also made some complimentary remarks with regard to the work being done by the Lodge and its officers. District Secretary Frank Webster gave a few interest- ing statistics concerning the District and his remarks were listened to with evident appreciation.—The following brethren took part in the " social " part of the proceedings :—P.G. J. Willett, P.G. A. Pemberton, Prov.G.N. Lot Brooks, P.G.A. Cotterill, P.G. T. Forbes, Bro. Seed and P.P.G.11. Alban Boyle. Bro. B. A. Lloyd gave a short but capital illusionist enter- tainment which highly delighted the brethren, and Bro. William Pemberton ably presided at the piano. SUGAR IS DNARER.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

LADY BRUNNER AND THE MAY FESTIVAL. Lady Brunner had promise( to crown the May Queen at Runcorn's festival to-day (Saturday), but in conse- quence of the tragic death of her son-in-law she has intimated that she cannot fulfil her engagement.

PUBLIC-HOUSE MUSICIAN AND HIS CHILDREN. At Runcorn' on Monday, Albert, Ravenscroft was sentenced to two months' hard labour for neglecting his seven children. Th 3 prisoner had lost situation after situation through losing time. Lately the children had been caught begging, and the police found the house without food and almost destitute of furniture and clothing, and in a very filthy condition. Superintendent Ennion said prisoner was in the habit of playing the piano at public-houses and drinking heavily.

SUDDEN DEATH IN A TRAIN. Samuel Blinston, a middle-aged man, residing in Forster-street, Widnes, died whilst journeying to Liver- pool from Widnes in the 5.7 train on Saturday night. He seemed to be in his usual spirits when he got into the train at Widnes, but was later noticed by a fellow- passenger to be in a state of collapse. Upon arrival at Ditton the guard's attention was called to the man's condition, and he was removed to Widnes. Dr. Hutchinson was sent for,but Bilnston expired before his arrival. The deceased was very highly respected, and followed the occupation of a coal merchant. SOVEREIGN INSTEAD OF A SHILLING.

At Widnes on Monday, Mary Hatton, a servant girl, residing in Caroline-street, was charged with stealing a sovereign, the property of Mary Jones, residing in Ann-street. At eight o'clock on Friday night Jones, when paying her for cleaning, gave her a sovereign in mistake for a shilling. The girl went away, spent ss. on a new hat and Ss. at the fair. When arrested next morning, she said she knew nothing about it ; but eventually told the truth, and is. 3d. was found on her. The bench treated her as a first offender, and placed her under the care of a probation officer for six months, and ordered her to refund the money as soon as possible. LICENSING BUSINESS AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Transfer Sessions on Monday, before Sir Richard Brooke and Mr. T. D. Timmins, William Thomas Richardson, licensee of the Aston Arms, Aston, applied for sanction to the making of a billiard room, and the consequent alterations to the hotel. Superin- tendent Ennion raised no objection. He said the police would have better supervision. Sanction was granted. —The following transfers of licences were approved : Nelson Inn, from Thomas H. Warder to James Jolley ; Manchester House, from James Jolley to Enock Tomlinson ; the Blue Bell beerhouse, from Michael , Riley to William Wittiugton ; and the Village Inn, ' Weston, from Mary Ann Hulse to John Carter. Mr. F. A. Lake appeared for Jolley and Tomlinson. WIDNES MAN'S LINGERING DEATH. Joseph Hargreaves, aged twenty-six, fitter's labourer ' 59, Kent-street, Widnes, died on Friday night last. On the 2nd of May, 1907, deceased was working at the Broughton Copper Works, Ditton. He was on a ladder adjusting the belting on the shaft, when the ladder slipped and he fell to the ground, striking an iron bar with his back. He was conveyed to Widnes Accident Hospital,where he remained for twelve days. Hargreaves was then removed to Whiston Workhouse Hospital,where he remained for another six weeks. He was afterwards taken home and attended by local doctors, and was eventually taken to the Royal Southern Hospital, Liver- pool, where an operation was performed, remaining in that institution for another sixteen weeks. He was ' brought home again, and, despite tho care of three local doctors, he gradually sank, and died from exhaus- tion. NEW WIDNES VICAR. The Bishop of Liverpool has appointed the Rev. Horace John Gibbins, M.A., 8.D., to the vacant_livin,, of St. Paul's, Widnes, in succession to the Rev. D. E. Morton, who held the benefice since 1901. Mr. Gibbins graduated with honours from Exeter College, Oxford, including Hasker Sch. 1380-91, first class Mod. 1391, B.A. (third class Lit. Hum.) 1803, second class Theology 1891, Wycliffe Hall, 1894, M.A., 1893, B.D. (Ox.) 1904, Ordained by the Bishop of St. Alban's deacon 1894, priest 1899, Mr. Gibbins held curacies at Waltham Abbey for two years, then St. Matthew's, Croydon, till 1891, whoa he was senior tutor Caurch Missionary College, Islington, London, till 1903, which saw him appointed vice-principal Bishop's Hostel, Liverpool, where in a quiet and very modest way, he has made a deep impression. A man of great learning; Mr. Gibbins preaches thoughtful and deep discourses, which are , keenly appreciated by his hearers. Consequently he was much sought after as a preacher on anniversaries and special occasions, and he has occupied a great number of pulpits in the different Liverpool churches.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

ACCIDENT IN A CRECEr MATCif. Mr. C. Porter, whilst playing in a cricket match between Newton and St. Helens on Saturday, had the misfortune to have his collar bone dislocated. TRICkiIEiIY AT EATILESTOWN.

Frederick Edwards, of no settled abode, was com- mitted to the Liverpool Quarter Sessions, at the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, for stealing by means of a trick two sums of money from two shop- keepers named Currey and Guthrie, at Elrlestown, on April 23rd. PLUCCZY RESCUE FROM TilE CANAL.

On Saturday morning two children named Ernest and Albert Pill (sons of Mr. Pill, Bridge-street, Earles- town), aged two and four years, wandered down to the canal side and fell in. Fortunately three gentlemen, Mr. Mather, Mr. Williams and Mr. Spolliswood, were walking along the canal bank at the time. Mr. Spollis- wood immediately dived into the water and brought one child to the surface, while Mr. Williams succeeded in grasping the other one as he rose in the water. Mr. Mather rendered first aid and brought them round, and they were conveyed home, when Dr. Valentine was called in to attend them, and the children have now almost recovered from the effects. BRUNSWICIi. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY. i The Bronswick-road Mission Sunday School anniver- sary was held on Sunday. At the morning service an II address was given by Mrs. Valentine, to parents,teachers and scholars,special music being rendered by the infants. At the afternoon service, a service of song, entitled "The Outcome of a Day," was rendered by the choir and children,under the conductorship of Mr. G.Rydeard, the reader being Mr. W. Gilby, of Ashton. At the evening• service the preacher was Mr. W. Gilby, and special music was rendered by the children. The services were well attended and the collections, which were in aid of the Sunday Schools, realized .E2O I7s.

GUILD ENTERTAINMENT. Last Thursday evening the scholars attending the Guild held in St. Peter's school gave a most enjoyable entertainment in the Town Hall. The first part consisted of items given by the children. and helpers (Guild teachers). The opening chorus "The laundry maids " was splendidly rendered by six little girls who washed the clothes and hung them on the line in correct style. This was followed by a dance performed by eight girls dressed as gipsies, who danced quite nicely with tambourines. Miss Mabel Braddock sang a sweet song entitled "The babes in the wood." tad several boys whistled to musical a.corapaniments. Next 'followed a screaming sketch entitled " ti?anted, a , wife." The audience were kept in roars of laughter from beginning to end, and all the parts were per- formed in a highly creditable manner. The second half of the programme was given by the Newton Pierrots, who are making quite a name in the entertain- ment world by the splendid performances they have given in aid of various charities. Every item was deservedly encored. The concert was given in aid of the Guild, which was organized by the late curate (the Rev. A. E. Bass) and has been so successfully carried on, and has done such good work throughout the winter. MARRIAGE OF MR. E. L. VICARS.

An event of considerable importance to this district was the marriage which took place at St. George's Church, Edgbaston, Birmingham, on Wednesday last week-, of Mr. Edward Lynton Vicars, only son of Mr. T. Vicars," The Knoll," Newton-le-Willows, to Miss Hilda Mabel Ketley, second daughter of Mr. J. Howard Ketley, of Bridge House, Trentham, Staffordshire. The church was beautifully decorated for the occasion, and the ceremony was witnessed by a largo and fashionable congregation. The bride was attended by eight brides- maids, mostly her own sisters, and a little brother as page boy. Mr. Vicars (Broad Green) was best man. The reception took place at the Grand Hotel, Colmore Row, Birmingham, over 200 attending. The presents were on view—some 300 in number—and it was estimated there was over £750 worth of silver. The employees of Messrs. T. and T. Vicars, Earlestown, sent a beautiful solid silver rose bowl, the office staff silver fish carvers, the heads of departments sending separate and choice gifts ; and congratulatory telegrams arrived from all parts of the country. Valuable presents were also received from Messrs. Ketley and Co.'s employees, Stafford. The 113 g was hoisted at the Earlestown Works, and on May 28th, when Mr. and Mrs. Vicars arrive home, the workpeople are to be feted at the TOwn Hall. The bride and bridegroom are taking a motor tour prior to a holiday in Paris. Oa returning they will reside at" The Beeches," Park-road, Newton

TRIPLE TRAGEDY NEAR NORTHWICEI. -MOTHER KILLS TIER TWO CIIILDREN. Hartford, a peaceful village near Northwich,-- was on Monday the scene of a painful tragedy, a mother killing her two little children and c yrimitting suioide. The children were drowned in a dolly tub and the mother's death was caused by poison, which had apparently been mixed in ginger beer. The tragedy took place in a little cottage on the Chester-road just beyond the church. Here resided Frances Gerrard, aged 43, with her husband, Charles, and family. The husband is farm bailiff to his mother at the Grange Farm, and has for twenty years filled the position of secretary to the local Tent of Rechabites. rThree of their seven children have commenced life on their own account and are away from home. The emaining four were Victor (12), 831 trice (10), Edith (7), and Margaret (21). The two youngest have been killed by their mother.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

BOWES COMPETITION FOR ST. HELENS PARKS ka The St. Helens Parks Committee have decided that notwithstanding the fact that their regulations expressly forbid the playing of games of any kind in the public parks for a trophy or gain of any kind, they will recommend the Council to approve of league or club matches or medal competitions being played on tho bowling greens of the local parks. The chairman of the Parks Committee (Councillor H. H. Peet) and deputy-chairman (Councillor T. Walsh) have pre- sented a cup for competition on the Corporation greens. ST. HELENS NEIGHBOURS.

Mary Ryan, a young married woman, of Silkstone- street, was remanded at St. Helens on Tuesday, on a charge of wounding another woman, named Mary Owen, a neighbour. The evidence was that at about a quarter past five on Monday afternoon a quarrel,which had been in progress for several days between the women,reached an acute stage. Mrs. Owen was passing the prisoner's door when it was alleged she was dragged inside and set upon with a poker. She received three wounds to the head, and had her fingers cut with a knife. By the time her husband reached the place she had been knocked senseless. He carried her home bleeding profusely, and she was removed to the Providence Hospital, and Mrs. Ryan was arrested by Inspector Sisson.—Prisoner, who denied using the poker, was remanded. ALLEGED FALSE PRETENCES AND TEETH. NOT READY FOR GOOD FRIDAY.

A charge of obtaining £1 17s. .1) y false pretences wan preferred at St. Helens on Monday against Walter J. ‘Vorawick, White-street, Widnes.—Mrs. Eliza Ashbrook, Island's-brow, Parr, said that on February 3 she went with her husband to Runcorn, and in the Masonic public- house they met Worswick, who said he was travelling for a firm of artificial teeth dealers. She told him she was thinking of having some teeth, but she had partly given the order to a firm in St. Helens. He offered to put the teeth in for £2 10s., which was less than the previous offer. Mrs. Ashbrook said if be would call at St. Helens during the course of the month she would give him the order. He called the Saturday following and took one tooth out. Later he took out other teeth, and she had altogether paid £1 17s. The teeth were proruised for the Thursday before Good Friday, but they had not been delivered.—Worswick pointed out that he had given every receipt in his own name and on his own stationery. He had quite a large number of orders to fulfil, and Mrs.tshbrook's teeth were in course of construction. H 'absolutely denied all intention to defrand.—The bench ordered a week's remand, and granted bail in £lO and two sureties of .£lO.

div.p: VOTES FOR WOMEN.
