div.head: Meeting in Support at Warrington.
div.p: Meeting in Support at Warrington.

There was a large attendance at a public meeting promoted by the Warrington Women's Suffrage Society and held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street on Monday evening. The Rev. W. Bracecamp presided and the speakers were Mrs. Alan Bright, of Liverpool, and Mr. W. Mason. The members of the committee present on the platform were Miss Massy, Mrs. Mc Gregor,Nlrs. Parker and Miss Waring (secretary). . The CHAIRMAN said he came there as a learner,thongh he had a great deal of sympathy with the object of the meeting. Mrs. ALAN BRIO riT said there had recently been a bye-election of which they had heard much in Man- chester. (Hear, hear and laughter). In that election there were sixteen different organizations at work, and these included three women's suffrage societies. If they asked the political agents what was the influence of these societies they would be told it was nothing, but if they asked the man in the street, who really was a better judge of what influenced votes than the political agent —(laughter)—ho would say that it was the women who threw out Mr. Churchill. If he were a good Liberal he would preface the word " women " by an adjective which was more forcible than polite. (Laughter). She claimed that other bye-elections where the Government candidates fared badly were also largely influenced by the ladies. ("Question.") Well, that mag the opinion of impartial observers. , The women at political elections had become a force to Ibe reckoned with. Formerly the women were cajoled by the Primrose League or ordered by the Women's Liberal Federation, but the time had come when the women had begun to work for the furtherance of their own sex an were not content to act merely in the interests of men. It is said that the majority of women did not want the vote. (Applause from a section of the audience.) It was very difficult to find out really what uumber of women did or did not want the vote. There was an enormous number of women to-day!who were afraid to speak out, sometimes from fear of their male relatives and sometimes from fear of their female relatives. If, however, a thing was right and logical and just it did not matter whether few or many wanted it. (Hear, hear.) There were a certain number of leisured or ignorant women who were opposed to the franchise, but the majority of thinking women and industrial women were in favour of enfranchisement. (Hear, hear.) Mrs. Bright argued in favour of the vote to women as a measure of justice and as a means of improving the conditions of employment of women. Gre it Britain was divided into four parties, and she would like te examine the chances of getting the vote from any of them. She was a good Liberal, but she was of the opinion that at present they had no hope from the Liberals. The Conservatives were opposed to the movement, and Mr. Balfour absolutely refused to receive a deputation on the question. When they came into power she was afraid they would fare little better than the Liberals had done. They had one or two excel- lent friends in the Irish Party, but the majority would have nothing whatever to do with them. In the Labour Party the rank and file were not in favour of women's suffrage. (A Voice - " Adult suffrage.") With regard to adtilt franchise, she was very much afraid that if a Bill were brought in with that object the House of Lords would never pass it and the word "manhood" would most likely replace the word "adult." The women would have to convince the majority of men that industrial women were suffering, and she had faith in the justice of Eng- lishmen that when they were aroused they would do justice. A great deal had been said about the militant tactics of certain women. Personally, she was not in favour of them, because, after all, women were not as strong as men, in regard to brute force, and it Was a mistake for women to play their weakest card. She did not think force was the best weapon. It was moreover, a mistake to think that causes advocated by forceful means always succeeded. She believed in holding meetings like the one they were holding there and in putting forward the jnstice and rights of their cause. If they could convert three-fourths of the women of England the Government would grant the measure in a few months. (Applause.) Mr. MASON said he esteemed it a great privilege to have that opportunity of giving his reasons as a man why be was in favour of women's suffrage. He repre- sented a profession where the majority of the workers were women and, after twenty years' experience, he could say that judged by any standard they might like to raise, the work of the woman was at any rate equal to that of the man in the same circumstances. In many cases it was undoubtedly superior. The remunera- tion paid, however, was altogether disproportionate to the remuneration paid to men. He believed that if woman's influence could be brought to bear in the administration of large departments like the Education Department, such anomalous conditions could be swept away. What was good for one section of the population was good for the whole. Women were quite as capable of voting intelligently as the men. There would not be more women making asses of themselves in the polling booth than men. (Laughter.) From the political and legislative point of view, women's views were totally ignored when laws were being framed. In the framing of laws relating to licensing, education. factories, and poor laws, the influence of women would be of benefit to the whole country. They would be perfectly safe in trusting local veto in the hands of women voters and the bother about the reformation of clubs would be speedily settled. (Laughter.) It did not matter to him whether a majority or a minority of the women of the land wanted a vote. There were some women, by no means the least intelligent, who wanted the vote, and they had a right to have it. (Applause.) He was tired of being told that the tactics of the militant section were pushing the mOvemett backward. Whatever they might have been guilty of, he would undertake to find a parallel from the behaviour of the opponents of the Licensing Bill. (Applause). Speeches or questions front opponents having been invited Mr. J. H. Jones read a long dissertation against women's suffrage. He pointed out that the women workers had benefited equally with the men from past legislation. Mrs. Alan Bright contended that women's wages would never be raised unless they had the vote. The vote was, however, not such an indispensable factor in the case. It was upon the strength of the trade unions rather than the vote that the amount of wages depended. Before giving the vote to women they should reflect seriously, as it would he a momentous Step. Mrs. BRIGHT, while twitting the last speaker on having entertained the audience with " quctations " contended that unless women had the vote their trade unions would not be able to accomplish the same work as the men's.

A member of the audience wished to know what per- centage of women workers would be entitled to vote if the franchise were extended to them on equal terms with men ? Mr. MasoN said he had not the statistics, but it would add about 1,500,000 to the present electorate. The Rev. C. HARVE V-COOK warmly supported women's snffeage, and with regard to the fear that the result might be that women would enter Parliament, he said if women could govern better than men, welt, let them do so. If women could beat the men, let the latter take their beating without any weeping or whin- ing. A resolution in favour of women's suffrage was ti.ien put to the meeting and carried by a large majority, there being between 30 and 40 dissentients. The meeting closed with a hearty vote df thanks to the Chairman, proposed by Ar. CARRUTHERS, seconded by Miss BROADBENT.

div.head: IN THE EIGHTEEN HUNDREDS. CRIMINAL CASES.
div.p: IN THE EIGHTEEN HUNDREDS. CRIMINAL CASES.
More Reminiscences by J. C. S.

Adverting to the frequency of the death punishment of law breakers of the criminal class in the Seventeen Hundreds, treated of in a previous paper, it may be assumed that the terrors of the death penalty were at that period less dreaded by convicted persons and that the general public, at a period prior to establishment of constabulary forces or of other organized systems of prevention and detection, deemed severe treatment and public executions necessary for protection against violence and robbery. Then also were judges le,x pained or troubled over the enforcement of the extreme statutory power given to them. I have witnessed in the second half of the Eighteen Hundreds a judge sobbing as he put on the black cap and in the ordinary words usual to the occasion directed public execution. ' It is related of a former judge—Alan Parke—that he was generous and amiable ; yet for all that he was " hanging judge." Upon an occasion of beigg on circuit it was found, after biz leaving the Assize Court and having left the Assize town, that a poor wretch con- victed of sheep stealing had not received sentence. Quick messengers were despatched and the learned judge was overtaken on his way to the next county. Return- ing to the judgment seat he apologized for the omis- sion and, mild in manner and terms, explained to the unfortunate prisoner the circumstances in which be inadvertently turned over two leaves of the printed calendar, thereby over-looking his name, and concluding his otherwise genial remarks, left him for public execution. All of the pre- sent generation will agree that capital punishment can only be held just in respect of acts of deliberate murder. The execution of criminals for less than wilful murder is not now permitted by the law. I was present in the Chester Assize Court when the lest death sentence was passed in this kingdom for an offence less then murder. The accused man was Martin Doyle, convicted of brutal usage, amounting to attempted murder, of his wife, who cave evidence against him in court. The manner of delivery of the sentence and the accompanying words by the judge, Baron Watton; clearly showed the determination to have the sentence carried out, and Doyle was publicly executed.

div.head: SUMMARY JURISDICTION.
div.p: SUMMARY JURISDICTION.

The recent paper on tha distribution of justice in the Seventeen hundreds named the more active of the local justices in that century. Examination of the list, as existing in the early Eighteen Hundreds, will evidence omission of several of the former names without altera- tion of names that remain familiar to the present generation. Thus Blackburne had succeeded to Black- borne, Lyon to Lyon, Patten to Patten. There were John Blackburne of Orford Hall and J. Blackburne of Mill Bank, Hollins Green ; Thomas Lyon of King- street in succession to John Lyon of King-street ; Thomas Patten of Warrington Pnd Peter • Patten of Bank Hall (now the Town Hall.) As the century advanced the Blackburnes removed to Hale, the Lyons to Appleton, and the Pattens to more distant parts. Other residential changes following led to additions of names to the Commission of the Peace for each of the two counties. Thus, Thomas Parr, from Winwick to Grappenhall flues ; William Hall, from Bank-street to Grappenhall Hall ; and at a later period William Stubs. from Church-street to The Elms, Dares- bury ; and Joseph Stubs, from Stanley-street to The Park, Frodsham (once the site of the ancient Frodsham Castle). There were also the two Stantons of Thel wall, Sir Gilbert Greenall, of Walton, and Edward Greenall of Wilderspool. Upon the passing of the Poor Law Acts in 15:32., county justices (they were all then of the county) became ex-officio guardians of the poor. In many ways, as of county and parish, government in some respects of licensing, in their powers over police and prisons and asylums, and practically at least in their powers over the grant of relief and the assessment of ratable heredita- ments and of their position of ex-officio guardians have justices by modern legislation been deprived ; yet withal their name, county and borough alike, is legion. It is unnecessary, neither would it be to this generation instructiee, to dwell upon present modes of local summary judicial jurisdiction. There will remain after this paper opportunity for reminiscence in relation to past exceptional experience acquired by the w Titer in his days of official participation with local magistrates procedure. The present observations upon summary modes ef punishment for minor offences will be con- cluded by a few words upon the once too frequent vac of
"THE STOCKS."

I remember reading many years back a letter pub- lished in the " W,rrington Guardian " written by the late Robert Garnett, of Pcnketh, inquiring " what had become of the stocks he remembered seeing in use in h:s youthful days?" It was in my mind to reply to th 3 query, yet somehow the occasion passed without my doing so. In now replying, it is as a matter of history, and I shall use names exactly as everybody did use them et the period of the event. It was in the Eighteen Thirties when " Johnny Kermode," a little 3lanxman, was the most popular of the three policemen Rating tinder Deputy Jones. Formerly the stacks (a frame of wood in which the legs of convicted drunkards were confined during a period of degradation and public exposure, the frame resting upon iron wheels) when in nse were placed at Market-gate, but on the treusfer of the market from Bridge-street to the Market-square, then called the Corn Market they were placed, when in use, by the fish stones near to the square. Now, it was as big a punishment to "Johnny Kermode " to keep him I standing in any one place for six successive hours as it was to the prisoners in his charge sitting for the same period in the stocks, and it happened upon the occasion of their last public use, when " Billy Dow "and his ' wife, hawkers pf fish—two wretches who would at the present day be confined in the workhouse imbecile wards—sat together in the stocks, that Johnny was missing at the unfortunate hour of the afternoon when school lads were released from neighbouring schools. When Johnny emerged from the neighbouring passage he fell into a very hot temper, flourishing his stick in the air and declaring he would lock up all con- cerned in the flight of the stocks and his prisoners. To the great delight of Billy Dow and his wife mischievous school lads had run with stocks and occupants from the fish stones across the Market-svare, through Lyme- street and Iforsemarket-street, into ‘Vinwick-street, where Johnny Kermode, guided by amused onlookers, overtook them and became reconciled to the position upon the voluntary offer of lads, who, of course," were not of those who bad done the mischief," to push the stocks hack to the fish stones. That was the last occa- sion of punishing Warrington drunkards by " public " use of the stocks. Their illegal use in the Eighteen Fifties, in a private way, may receive notice in a future paper. ADJOURNMENT OF ASSIZE.

Much dissatisfaction arose in the early part of the Eighteen Hundreds out of the continuous holding of the "Court of Oyer and Terminer, and of General Gaol Delivery," without adjournment of the business from the northern to the southern side of the county. Lan- caster in Assize time became a very busy county town, Vet a place dilncult and ex r 'naive be reached by .'jurors and others from the Mersey boundaries. An ever increasing effort was made by Liverpool, Manchester a-id Warrington to induce Parliament to provide for an adjournment to a more convenient r mtre. Upon the prospect of succc-sfel result further effort was made to have Warrington selected. Thus" At a meeting of the inhabitants of the town of Warriagton, held at the Sessions Room on Saturday, the 2 tth day of May, 1823, to consider the proper end most effectual means of promoting the objects of a petition latAy sent up to his Majesty's Government for obtaining an adjournment of the Assizes for the county of Lancaster to this town, Th.. James Haddock, in the chair, resolved t—l, ' That it is highly expedient to make increased exertions to obtain an adjournment of the County Assizes to the town of Whrrington '; 2, that a committee of nine inhabitants, together with the constables of the toss a. b 3 now appointed to take such steps as may appear pro- per for effecting the purpose, and that such committee do consist of the undermentioned gentlemen :—Thomas Lyon, Esquire, Mr. Glazebrooke, Mr. Nicholsou, Mr. J. Wagstaff, Mr. :John Clare, Mr. Greenall, Mr. Richard Turner, Mr. Edward Turner, Mr. John Piekmere, and that such committee have power to add to their number ' ; 3, that a deputation be sent up forthwith to co-operate with the deputations already gone thither from Liverpool and Manchester in the above object, and that Joseph Parr, Escinira, the senior constable, John Ireland Blackburne, Thomas Lyon, Peter Nichol- son, and Edward Turner, Esquires, be rc quested. to form such deputation and proceed to Town without delay, and that the deputation be instructed from time to time to correspond with the committee before appointed 4, that the Lord Lieutenant of the county and the Earl of Stamford and Warrington and Lord Lilford be respectfully requested to forward the object which the committee has in view' ; 5, that John Blackburn°, Esq., be most earnestly solicited to promote the prayer of the memorial lately presented by the inhabitants of this town, and that Lord Stanley, the members of the boroughs of Liverpool and Newton, and the members for the county of Cnester be also invited to co-operate with Mr. Black- burne thereon' ; 6, 'that a subscription he now entered into for the purpose of defraying the expenses of the deFtaticm now appointed and any other expenses which the committee may be of opinion ought to be paid thereout and that Mr. John Brandwood be appointed treasurer of such subscription.' The Chairman having retired, the unanimous thanks of the meeting were voted to him for his very proper conduct in the chair." AN EARLY EXECUTION.

It is unnecessary tia-r-ta-i;e-rPOOI- was selected as the place of adjournment, Ormskirk being at that time the place for holding Quarter Sessions. Unfortunately, following the completion of prelimin- aries enabling the hob'ing of a Court of Assize at Liverpool and the erection of a county gaol at Kirkdale, an early public execution was that of a Warrington man. The indictment upon which he had been tried was the alleged murder of Elizabeth Minshull, also assault and stealing from her person. The circum- stances, as detailed in evidence, pointed to the second- named offence as the main issue and that the act was

contributory to he death ; they also pointed to the larceny as an effort to conceal the main offence and further to cast suspicion upon an unknown ordinary thief. Conviction, however, in respect of any one of the three counts of indictment incurred liability to the death sentence. The act of stealing instead of contributing to escape from suspicion, resulted in establishing conclusive evidence of guilt. The man was seen to throw some article into the reservoir at the factory where he was employed. The waters were rim off and re silver box, taken from the person of Mrs. Minshull, was discovered. The jury found the prisoner, who was ably defended by counsel, guilty of the offences as set out in the indictment, and he was sentenced to death. I remember Mrs. Minshull,sister of Thomas Iligginson, licensee of the Legh Arms, an inn the site whereof was the entrance from the original Market-place into the present Market-street. The crime was committed in buildings within the curtilage of the inn after the hour of closing at night. I saw the witnesses for the prose- cution leave the Legh Arms on the morning of their departure by coach to the Court of Asbize. J. C. S.

div.head: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P.
div.p: MR. A. H. GROSFIELD, M.P.
OPENS A GROCERS' EXHIBITION AT MANCHESTER.
Commerce the Peacemaker.

On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, M.P. opened the seventh Northern Counties Grocers' and Allied Trades Exhibition in the St. James's Hall, Manchester. Organized and controlled by the Northern Council of Grocers' Associations and the Manchester, Salford and District Grocers' Association, the exhibition, which will continue until Thursday next, is undoubtedly the finest of its kind ever held in Manchester. To secure a record attendanc3 of the trade, the management had sent out by post 50,000 free tickets and, for the public benefit, 300,000 half-price coupons were circulated. There are nearly 120 stands, and whilst there is little in the exhibition which is new, some exceedingly pretty displays are made, and many of the stalls are quite artistic with their neat arrays of the thousand and one articles which the up-to-date grocer has to stock if he wishes to secure and retain the custom of the public. And not only has the grocer thus placed before him anything and eveiy- thing that he may want for his shop; there are m attendance ex' 3,rts who will give him the best passible advice as to how to attract customers by advertising devic3s. At many of the stalls visitors to the exhibition are able to sample the articles displayed, and if that and the very fine exhibition itself are not sufficient to retain int3rest entertainment may Le found in the music played by the Blue Hungarian Band. For people directly concerned in the trade numerous competitions have been arranged for the benefit of employer, manager and assistant.
OPENING CEREMONY. MR. CROSFIELD'S INTERESTING SPEECH.

There was a large attendance at the opening of the exhibition, Mr. J. P. Evans, of Birkenhead (president of the Northern Council) presiding. On the platform were many prominent representatives of the trade in the northern countie- Amongst the letters of apology for non-attendance WAS one from Mr. Winston Churchill and in submitting it, Mr. James Kendall (a 3retary of the Manchester, Salford and District Groceia' Association), expressed the hope that the President of the Board of Trade would emerge triumphant from his °le otoral struggle so that he might take up his itnport-,nt duties. (Applause). The Chairman said they had amongst them +hat afternoon a rneml nt of Parliamen. Mr. Crostleld who had travelled from London specially to open the exhibi- tion. (Applause). It was his (the chairmr-i's) duty to introduce Mr. Czosfleld to the audience, although he felt there was no need to introduce a Crostield in Lew: shire. (Applause.) The members of tht family were so well-known rid highly respected that it UTS only necessary to mention the raine in order to draw a large gathering like they had that day. The Noraiern Council comprised about 23 of the chief grocers' associations in that district, representing practi- cally the cream of the grocery trade in North Leiri- shire, and they were proud to see such a Poe exhibition as they had that dec. As grocers, they felt that the keenness of competition to-day was far in excess of anything which bed ever happened before. What with I the large company shops and the Co-operative move- ment, the individual grocer found it vet/ hard to make ends meet. He believed such institutions as that exhibi- tion where the production of the various menufacturc-, was brought before their eyes, must be of g. eat educa- tional value. They had a great deal of legis'ation nowadays in connection v,:th their tiade and, as Mr. C.osfleld would be able to tell them, no newer ti,an nineteen Bil's benring directly or indirectly upon the erocery trade came before committees of the Horse of commons last session. It behoved grocers to be well up in law as well as in chemistry if they were going to he successful in the future. (Applause.) Mr. Eyr•4 I ..hen called upon Mr. Crosfield to open the exbibitior
MR. CROSIHELD'S SPEECH. COMMERCE THE PEACEMAKER.

Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, 31.1'., who had a very cordial greeting, prefaced his remarks with an expression of t,.rnks to all those in authority in connection with the Giocei.f Association for their kindness in asking him to lrue to Manchester to open that strikingly hand- some and interesting exhibition. He could assure them that he sincerely felt it was a great honour to do to. He did not take the kindness and honour 09 paid to himself personally, but inasn3uch as for close upon a century Manchester had always been the greatest market for the manufacture with which his family had for seve.al generations been connected, no doubt that fact might have weighed a little with some of those who had invited him, and he cordially thanked them for the priN;lece extended to him. Hewes particularly indeht-d to his friend Mr. Kendal for the trouble he had taken to post hint up in the objects which the promoters of the exhibition had in view. One of them no doubt was to bring the producer and the distributor into close contact, which would unquestionably be to the advantage of them both. (Hear, bear). I, WiLLIAM STEVENSON, of 19 Rirkstone-street, Bradford, in the County of Yorks, do solemnly and a' ncerely cicllaie as follows : My son. Eraest Stevenson, l.'s for many years been a great sufferer from Rheumatism. Whenever be was seized with an atflck of this complaint, he was forced to throw up his work and lay in bed, often remaining in bed for weeks at a time,and throughout these periods he constantly suffered the most intense pain and agony. When in this condition, it was impossible for him to move about, or to do anything to assist himself. He screamed like a child at the slightest movement,and even the act of anyone walking across the room in which he lay was sufficient to arouse the pain and cause him the most excruciating agony. On one of 1315 more recent attacks he was laying in bed for about siz weeks, utterly helpless, and although I obtained for him the best medical advice I could get, he was never free from pain during the whole of this long time, and it seemed that he was likely to become a' chronic invalid. I almost despaired of his ever becoming fully restored to-heelth, and was content if the doctoia could patch him up for the time, in ordea to afford at least a little Interval between the attalks. In the month of February, 1908, he was again stricken with this malady. I was at a complete loss to know what I could do or get in order to alleviate his suffer- ings, when my eyes providentially fell upon a news- paper paragraph in which Liquid Barkola Compound, used with certain other ingredients, was recommended as a cure for Rheumatism. Although I had but little faith after the experiences I ban had with regard to other remedies and medical advice in the past that any- thing could have much effect, yet I procured a bottle of the prescription which I had seen. It was made up as follows : Liquid Barkola Compound 1 ounce. Tincture of Gentian ' 1 ounce. Syrup of Rhubarb 1 ounce. Syrup of Ginger 5 ounces. The first bottle gave my son immediate relief, and seemed to entirely remove the pain. I continued to give him the preparation until he bad taken three , bottles, when-ell effects of his illness left him, and he I seemed to have regained r3rfect health and to be as well as he had ever been. Several weeks have since elapsed, during which time my eon has pursued his usual o ocoupatio without inconvenience of any kind, and he has continued in this satisfactory condition, and to-day feels as if every trace of the dreaded Rheumatism had left his system for ever. 7ENT. A STORY FOR CHILDREN.
Long, long ago a robin and a butterfly talked over their troubles one day. "How much nicer it would be to live in a house, as men do I " said. the robin.

" There's a black cloud in the sky, and I'm sure it's going to rain, I'll have to cuddle up under the leaves, and my feathens will be damp. I fear I'll take cold and lose my loice." "I have to hide away, too, when it. rains," said the butterfly. " 'Twould be a great pity if the water washed off my lovely powder, and. a big shower might drown me. _ . _

Miss Butterfly, was quick-witted. "Why not go to live in that house now t The window's open." And she flew in at once. The robin was more cautious. He lighted an the window- sill, and peeped around. "I don't see any place for a nest."

Pshaw I You don't need a nest in a houee,', said his gay little friend. So Master Robin flew in, and perched on the first thing he found, which was a book; but he looked homesick. Miss Butterfly fluttered to a quill-pen, and made believe it was a flower.

Pretty soon there were sounds, and the robin listened as hard as he could. "0 papa!" a child's voice said. "Look there! - Sh-sh Keep still! You'll scare them! What a beautiful butterfly for your collection! And papa, mayn't I have the bird in a cage? I'd like a robin with my canary." A man's voice answered low, "Run around outi3ide then, deary, and close the window softly, so they can't get out." Master Robin's brains were wide awake now. He spoke quickly: "That man's an en—onto-- well, I can't say it; but he's crazy on insects, and -he'll stick a pin through you, my lady. And that girl thinks she'll put me in a cage! I guess not! Let's fly!"

Out they flew, just as the little maid's hand touched the sash. They heard her cry of dis- appointment as they dashed by her. ' "0 papa they just went out like a flash; and they're both gone!" But Master Robin and Miss Butterfly laughed happily to be out again in the free air. The black cloud .was gone, and the warm spring sun was shining on the garden-beds of crocus and hyacinth. How beautiful it was out of doom! Living in a house was not to be com- pared to it. "Better be content Where- our Maker meant us to live," said Miss Butterfly. A wise after- thought of the highty-tighty little creature!

THE AFTER-SHADOW OF GAUCHERIE.

The only real shadow of early shyness is the quite disproportionate amount of unhappiness that conscious gaucherie brings with it. When I was an Eton boy, I was staying with a country squire, a most courteous old gentleman with a high temper. The first morning, I contrived to come down a minute or two late for prayers. There was no chair for me. The Squire suspended his reading of the Bible with a deadly sort of resignation, and. made ri gesture to the portly butler. That functionary rose from his own chair, and with loudly creaking boots carried it across the room for my acceptance. I sat down, covered with confusion. The butler returned ; Rlid two footmen, who were Pitting onn little form, made reluctant room for him. The butler ; sat down on one end of the form, unfor- tunately before his equipoise, the second footman, had taken his place at the other end. The result was that I the form tipped up, and a cataract of flunkies poured downaipon the floor. There was a ghastly silence; then the Gadarene herd slowly recovered itself, and resumed its place. The Squire read the chapter in an accent of suppressed fury, while the remainder of the party, with handkerchiefs pressed to their faces, made the most unaccountable sounds and motions for the rest of the proceedings. I was really camparatively guiltless, but the shadow of that horrid event sensibly clouded the whole of my visit.—From' At Large," in the " Cornhill Magazine "for May. WINSTON CHURCHILL ON MAN'S DUTY. I am clearly of opinion that no man has a right to be idle, whoever he be or wherever he lives. He is bound to go forward and take an honest share in the general work of the world. And I do not except the African native. To a very much larger extent than is often recognised by some who discuss those questions, the natives are industrious, willing to learn, and capable of being led forward. Live for a few weeks, as I have done, in close association with the disciplined soldiers of the King's African Rifles, or with the smart soldiers of the Uganda Marine, and it seems wonderful to contrast them with I the population from which they have emerged. How strong, how good-natured, how clever they are! How proud their white °Ulcers are of them ! What pains they take to please the travellers whom they escort ; how frankly they are delighted by a word of praise or thanks! Just and honourable discipline, careful educa- tion, sympathetie comprehension, are all that is needed to bring a very large proportion of the native tribes of East Africa to a far higher social level than that at which they now stand. And why should men only be taught to be soldiers? Is war always to have the best of everything? Cannot peaceful industry be made as attractive, be as highly organised, as carefully studied es the combined use of deadly weapons? "Why," as Ruskin asks, " cannot men take pride inbuilcling villages instead of only carrying them ?"—From the Strand Magazine," May. DARWIN'S GRANDSON AS NOVELIST. Among the twenty-five splendid complece stories which are appearing in the May issue of the " Grand Magazine of Fiction "one of the most noteworthy is a tragic little story entitled " Stapleton Pageant," by Bernard Darwin. . This is especially interesting as the author is the grandson of the illustrious naturalist, and although he is already well-known in other branches of literature, this is his first incursion into the realms of fiction. In the same number Robert Blatchford, editor of the " Clarion," contributes a powerful story entitled "The Fiery Pitt " ; while another fine story is "The Seventh Child of a Seventh Child," by Miss A. M. Garstin, the sister of Sir William Garstin.
MR. FRANK T. BELLEN ON THE MARINER'S

COMPASS. "Nothing in the navigational equipmen:, of a ship has been the subject of more anxious scientific research or receives more jealous care than the mariner's compass," says Mr. Frank T. Bullen in an interesting article on " Some Obscure Sea Perils "in the May " Windsor Magazine." -" The popular notion of the compass needle always pointing north and south is—well, more inaccurate than even popular notions usually are. Even under the most favourable conditions there are only certain places upon the surface of the earth where the compass needle does point north and south, and it is quite safe to say that such conditions are never found on board any ship. But we must go farther and say that no more unfavourable position could be found for a compass than on board of a modern teamship, which is a complicated mass of steel, all tending to draw the compass needle from its allegiance to the magnetic pole of the earth, warring influences which must needs be counteracted by all sorts of devices which hedge round the instrument by an invisible wall of conflicting currents of magnetism. And as if this were not enough, there are now huge dynamos to be reckoned with, producing electric currents for all sorts of purposes on board. In tke midst of these mystic currents the poor little compass needle, upon which the mariner depends for his guide across the trackless deep, hangs suspended like one shrinking saint surrounded by legions of devils."

div.head: DELINEATOR.
div.p: THE DELINEATOR.

"The Delineator" is a high-class fashion paper which only needs to be known to be appreciated. It is published monthly at 6d. and the May number is now in the hands of the newsagents. At this time of the year when most feminine minds are much occupied with their wardrobes, it is a particularly interesting number. There are designs for gowns suitable to all occasions, and every age, but particular mention should be made of the charming morning frocks, in which the detail and finishing touches, that count for so much, are well within the scope of most home dressmakers, and the patterns very reliable. Then there is the usual article on " What they are wearing in Paris," which is interesting as a forecast of what we are going to wear here, a pretty page of hats, and another entitled "At the point of the needle," which is for the home embroideress. The literary portion is occupied by a pleasant serial of Mrs. Burton Harrison's and other items. After which there are some cooking recipes and an article on hygiene. AN ESSAIE IN PRAYSE OF BEER. The first thing that appears in men who love their beer is their likeness one to another. Many love Sherry Wine, many stand by Port or Burgundy; yet is the man of Port no liker to his fellow than to the man of Sherry. Not 40 with Beer. Beer can be loved only by such as are of a certain temper of mind. Such be those who have in their souls something of contemplation, philo- sophy, content. Beer differeth from beer almost as much as they that drink it from each other. The gulf between small, watered ale and Old is well-nigh as wide as that between the Initiate and him that drinketh for the stomach's sake. Yet net altogether, for both have in them something of the essence. Nay, Small Beer is not at all times to be despised. A right pleasant thing to one that toileth at midsummer is a gallon jar of wickered earthenware, lurking beneath some shady hedgerow. Oft will he betake him to the thin amber creature leaving his swathe and quaffing great rivers of refreshing Swipes. Some there he who tell of two, nay, of three gallons that so have followed one another on a July day ; but such, methinks be mendacious persons, men of false pride, for what glory lieth in making of one own's self a cask for Swipes? Nay, hardly should this service of small ale be counted with the noble purposes of good Beer. And what beer is like Old Ale—which in some places is known as Old Beer. 'Tis said, indeed, that queen Bess ever broke her fast with strong Ale, a Royal ensample which the prudent Beer-Lover will humbly set aside. At midday a pint pot of Mild Beer Ilanketh well a piece of cheese with bread and pickling cabbage, nor will it shame a more Sicilian meal. Yet let it not be thought that a certain measure of beer should be drunk each day at a certain time. The Votary will rather drink his pint at midday, his pint at night, and no more, except he be much at large.—From an article in the May Pall Mall Magazine."

div.p: SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS.

CREASOTE IN GASTRIC AFFECTIONS. According to Dr. Theodore Zanger, of Zurich, the present tendency to think that the larger the dose of this drug the better in phthisical cases is by no means justified by experience, for the best results are often ob- tained with very small doses indeed. He be- lieves that their beneficial effect is due to thele action on th tomach, causing it to do it work better, and so to improve the nourishment of the system. lie finds that in many cases of purely gastric airection§, with or without diarrhrea, or other intestinal symptoms, minute doses of creosote will often succeed when other remedies have failed.

DECOMPOSING ROCK BY ELECTRICITY. The felspar of granite and other rocks is broken up by, the slow processes of nature to supply the needful soda and potash to the soil. Rain charged with carbon dioxide con- verts the silicates of soda and potash which occur in the felspar into carbonates, 'and these are washed out into the soil. This, however, is a slow process, and a quicker method of extracting these necessary ingre- dients for the soil has been -devised in -the United States. The impatient farmer can now have the felspar of his subsoil or rocky substratum decomposed, and his soil en- riched with potash and soda by means of electricity.

div.head: SPICES AND DIGESTION.
div.p: SPICES AND DIGESTION.

Although the use of spices for the pur- poses of heightening the flavour of food is al- most universal, it is generally recognised that their influence on digestion is detri- mental. Experiments tend to prove, accord- ing to the Indian Lancet, that while spices stimulate the motor functions of the stomach, they progressively impair the secre- tory functions, and in the long run inhibit the production of hydrochloric acid. On the whole, therefore, the ingestion of spices hin- ders rather than accelerates digestion, though an exception may be made in respect of per- sons in whom slowness of digestion is due to a deficiency of muscular activity on the part of the stomach, and also possibly of the vie- Aims of hyperacidity.

div.head: WATER VAPOUR ON MARS.
div.p: WATER VAPOUR ON MARS.

Professor Lowell's announcement that he has discovered in the spectrum of Mars in- dications that the planet is very rich in water vapour is a return, .says the Globe, to the opinions of the older observers. For nearly all the early students of its spectrum thought it indicated an atmopshere like our own, but containing even more water vapour. During the opposition of 1892, however, the planet was carefully observed by Professor Camp- bell, of the Lick Observatory, and from its spectrum he inferred that its condition was like that of the Moon. In other words, that it had no water vapour, and, in fact, no atmo- sphere. From a study of the Kinetic theory of gases applied to the atmospheres of planets, Dr. Johnstone Stoney concluded that water cannot remain on Mars.

div.head: PRODIGIES AND GENIUS.
div.p: PRODIGIES AND GENIUS.

Discussing the history of mathematical prodigies, Professor G. A. Miller, of tha Uni- versity of Illinois, remarks that the greatest arithmetical prodigy on resort was a Ger- man named Dasa, born at Hamburg in 1824. He was a kind of human calculating, machine, able to carry on enormous calculations in his head, but nearly incapable of understanding the principles of mathematics, and of very limited outside ability. On the other hand, the celebrated German mathematician; Gauss, was not only one of the greatest men tal calculators on record, but at the same time a man of vast mathematical, genius. The general conclusion is that eltraordinary powers of mental calculation have no neces- sary connection with the possession of genius, or of great general ability.

div.head: SLOW MENTAL RIPENING.
div.p: SLOW MENTAL RIPENING.

Noil infrequently those mentalities that ripen the slowest last the longest, and often the history of great men has been per- sistent neglect and worldly coldness until forty or more years have passed before their greatness has been conceded by their con- temporaries. Truly, "the life history of a great genius is almost invariably one of a sad and sombre tone, a walk apart from the beaten path." Such are the words of one who should know what the "doers of deeds must endure. Be this as it may, writes W. A. Newman Dorland in the Century, it is now recognised that many of the finest achievements in business, statesmanship, lite- rature, and in all activities have been wrought by men long past sixty. Writes one: "No strong man will accept sixty as the arbitrary limit of his ambition and working ability."

div.head: ONE SERUM FOR ALL DISEASES.
div.p: ONE SERUM FOR ALL DISEASES.

According to the usual practice of serum therapeutics there is a special serum for each disease. This is prepared from the blood of an animal which has been inoculated with the virus of the disease, and become resistant to it. Professor Deutschmann, of Hamburg, however, claims to have discovered a serum which will do for all diseases. To prepare this, animals are given gradually increasing doses of yeast in their. food. The serum of their blood is then found to possess valuable properties. It aids and strengthens the cells in their conflict with disease germs. Accord- ing to Dr. Friedlieb, who gives an account of Professor Deutschinann's method in Um- schau, the serum has been successfully used in twenty-four cases of pneumonia. It has also cured five cases of contagious sore throat. In some cases it is found that yeast can be administered directly to the patient as a part of his diet with the same beneficial results. The cells of the blood seem thereby trained to a greater resisting power. Cases of car- buncle and contagious local catarrhs have been successfully treated in this way. When there are febrile symptoms, however, it is found better to use the serum. •

div.head: WHY A CAT FALLS ON ITS FEET.
div.p: WHY A CAT FALLS ON ITS FEET.

A problem of antique but abiding interest Is revived by M. C. Hartmann, who has con- , strueted an experimental model in order to shew why a cat always falls on its feet. It is one of the laws of mechanics that a body or a system of forces cannot set itself in rota- tion as a whole. If one part of it begins to rotate another part must rotate in a reverse direction as a compensatory force. A simple example of this is furnished by the experi- ment of twirling an oar in the rowlock of a boat (without allowing the oar to touch the water); the boat will begin to rotate in a direction opposite to that of the rotating oar. New at first sight it might appear that the cat defied this law of mechanics, since in falling it seems always able to rotate t its body so that its feet come undermost. But M. Hartmann shews reason for supposing that a cat is really an example of compensatory ro- tation. He has made a model of a primitive cat but of cardboard. The cat is a cardboard cylinder with four drumsticks, or ,reds, stuck in it for legs. On the inner side of the cylinder, furthest from the forelegs, he has a species of tail, also of cardboard, which is mounted on a strong movable iron wire. This iron wire is the termination of the axis of a spring concealed in the body of the cat. This spring can only be released and allowed to come into play when one looses a , string which comes out of the cardboard cat's stomach. M. Hartmann hangs his cat ,by this string -to that its four feet point upwards. When the string is cut the cardboara cat will fall, but at the same time the spring will be released, and as it conies into play the iron wire and the tail attached to it will begin to rotate with considerable speed. If the height of the fall is sufficient, and the dimensions of the apparatus and the 4trength of the spring are appropriate, the cardboard cat as it rotates will always fall on its feet. Thus, evidently the reason a cat always falls on its feet is that it rotates its tail with sufficient vehemAnei3 to produce the desired mechanical results. On this hypotheslt. a cat without a tail if dropped from a convenient height mhould be unable to regidate its fall.

div.head: PARLIAMENT'S LEAD FOR THE PEOPLE.
div.p: PARLIAMENT'S LEAD FOR THE PEOPLE.
LETTER FROM MR. GROSFIELD, M.P. Legislative Progress and the Licensing Bill.

Sir,—Since I last wrote to you we have chanced our Pilot, the beloved Leader of the Liberal Party having passed away amid tributes of esteem or affection, or both, of which one had evidence from people in every rank of society, of every shade of political opinion, and far from limited oven to one nationality. Once more there has been the solemn pageantry of a great funeral in Westminster Abbey, the sombre gravity of which was relieved by the exquisite beauty of the music and voices. The meeting afterwards in the House of Commons will be memorable for the speech of Mr. Asquith which was exceptionally fine because of the absolute truth of what he said about our late and revered chief. The same thing struck me about the meeting of our Party at the Reform Club, presided over by Sir John Brunner, and the speech which Mr. John Ellis then delivered. Perhaps it has been less widely read than Mr. Asquith's, but I have seldom listened to an address so stirring and, impressive, and that just because of its simplicity and absolute truth, which everyone in the room, of every shade of opiniononust have felt. . _
At that meeting it is unnecessary to say the choice of Mr. Asquith as

div.head: TIE LEADER OF OUP. PARTY
div.p: TIE LEADER OF OUP. PARTY

was endorsed with very great heartiness. Not only the speech in the House in which he paid the beautiful and truthful tribute to Sir Henry, to which I have just alluded, but every speech he has so far delivered, and his conduct of affairs gives evidence day after day of the pre-eminent ability, energy, and the marvellous power of concentrated mental force which he possesses. The long deep-toned roar of applause which greeted him when he rose to make his first speech as a Party Leader in the House—on the introduction of the Licensing Bill—was a truly significant ovation and one not speedily to be forgotten. This afternoon,listening to his really splendid and interesting speech on introducing the Budget, I could not but recall the remark an: American once made to Morley about John Stuart Mill, , whose mind, he said, worked as smoothly as some perfect piece of machinery. What people in the House have come to realise of late years is, that besides high intellectual power, there is warmth and kindly good nature under a somewhat formal exterior, which of course is all tending to increase the enthusiasm with which the Party is undoubtedly welcoming his accession to the Leadership. Everyone is of course pleased that Lloyd George and Churchill now occupy these high positions in the State and is offering them congratulations. Colonel Seely has made a first-rate start, and we expect yeomen ser- vice for the party in the future from that very cheery and capable man, who whether on the golf links or in the House has always lots of "go ' in him. Great things in the future may also be expected from Master- man, and neither in the case of him nor of Colonel Seely shall we be disappointed. Having alluded to golf, it just occurred to me that what in Lancashire we should call

" UTE kT has just been performed in the House of Commons, and who of us that hails trom Lancashire is going to forget, even in London, the splendid cricketing traditions of the County of the Red Rose. Therefore, I hope your i readers will not look askance at my metaphor even n a political letter. lam merely alluding to the fact that while this Licensing Bill is of course encountering 'tierce and determined opposition, on the other hand some of the most important work of this Government is really most heartily approved of by men of all parties, so that it is no exaggeration to say that three extremely important Bills tabled in the Horse of Commons in a single week were heartily welcomed throughout the House without distinction of party. Mr. Birrell gave us a University Bill for Ireland, so solving the problem which has vexed statesmen for a hundred years. Mr. Burns introduced his Housing Bill, which for the first time makes "Town Planning " possible for Municipalities. And then Mr. Lloyd-George after mouths of brilliant diplomacy, laid before the Commons the scheme for purchasing the London Docks and so re-organising that great and growing Port. If I may continue with another and similar cricketing metaphor, I would say that each of those Bills " hits the middle stump" and that three of them in one week is a record which any Government may well be proud of. Our good friend Sir John Brunner told us at the meeting at the Reform Club, to which I have referred, that the Liberal Party should have a Trade policy to set off against the specionx, and I will add, pretty thoroughly reckless promises of Tariff Reformers. Mr. Lloyd George has of course been taking that line and I venture to think that Liberals ass whole are thoroughly in accord with that policy. The Patents Act—already bearing fruit in the establishment of British Factories on British soil,—and the Port of London Bill are both cases in point ; and the abolition of preferential rates for foreign produce and manufacture on our railways, and the question of dealing with Urban rating, will both follow in good time, and both serve to put this policy into good and useful practice. 1311 t YT3 have 494 Illor Mr, Editor, to write you about

THE LICENSING Mil, which, as your readers all know, we have just recently passed through its Second Reading by a magnidet and no less significant majority. As I think you know I have always avoided what Tennyson calls " falseness of extremes" in dealing with the question of the Liquor Trade. The Bill as it stands is a draft sub- mitted for discussion and no doubt to some extent for amendment. lam not called upon at this stage to talk about its details ' ' we are concerned alone with its main principles. The Division Lobby has shown that on these main principles our party is united and deter- mined,and that we have in addition the hearty support of every section of those members who are the more special representatives of Labour—though even in a letter like this I deprecate even by implication, suggesting that there is any real division between genuine Liberalism and the true and best interests of Labour in the long run, and I well know that some of the best Liberal Labour men in the house—as distinguished from cer- tain revolutionary Socialists—are of the same opinion. And so in this bard-fought battle on behalf of reason- a'-‘le temperance and the just and legitimate rights of the nation, Liberals and Radicals, and Liberal Labour Members, as well as Members of the Independent Labour Party, are all working splendidly together, and just as during the whole of the Second Beading Debate opinion in favour of the Bill strengthened day by day in the House of Commons, so I am absolutely certain that whatever prejudice there may be in some constituencies at the outset, as a rather complicated issue gets more and more thoroughly understood in the country, the weight of opinion in the long run will be for the Bill, and strongly for it too. , I don't think we should overlook the debt we owe to the Churches which have given us great help in this Reform, and in Warrington we are under a special 1 obligation to the Bishop of Liverpool, who has been so keenly criticised for his public spirited work. I do not want to make this letter too long, but as the subject is of such importance, perhaps I should lay before your readers
FIVE DEFINITE POINTS all of them arising out of recent discussions on the Bill :

(1) A reduction in the number of public-houses is urgently needed. It was arranged for even in Mr. Bil four's Act. It will reduce the brewer's cost of distribution by getting rid of redundant houses, many of which aro often run at a loss ; and It will of course at the same time promote temperance. I know that last assertion is disputed, but after all in a very half-hearted fashion. Thorough investigation has long since settled tho question as to whether an exces- sive number of public-houses in thickly populated areas, does or does not increase the amount of drinking and misery in those areas, and all the evidence one hears from people practically acquainted with these things in our large cities, bears out the contention of the Liberal party in this matter. (2) If ever we are to have free houses, run not as drinking saloons merely, but as reasonable and pleasant resorts for working men of an evening, we must put a "time " upon the present monopoly I value of licences. By all means let us make the " time limit" a geneums one. This will be a very great reform to carry, and I for one frankly confess am in favour of carrying it on generous terms. That after all is a matter of simple arithmetic, but I do feel that this " time limit " must be final once it is fixed. Then we shall have better beer, the freedom of the licensed victualler, and the restoration of general catering, all of which after all depend on this question of the " time limit." (3) It is not the fault of Liberals if the licensed victnaller has not yet received proper compensation when his house is closed. We hope to put that right before the Bill leaves the House of Commons. Our clause at present is vague ; it grants to the publican "compensation for loss of business," a phrase which is pretty certain to be more carefully defined in the Committee stage. (-I) Next a word on thequestion of Unemployment in connection with this Bill. Men like Mr. Vivian, Mr. Harvey, Mr. Shackleton, Mr. Henderson and other leading representatives of Labour like them, don't tell us that this Bill is going to create unemployment. On the contrary they repudiate the suggestion. The truth is, as the public are beginning to realise, that licensed houses are constantly changing hands. Speak- ing from memory I believe the transfers are some- thing like ten thousand a year, but I cannot at the

moment refer to confirm that figure, and it may be over the mark. But it is a fact that there is a regrettably high wastage in the liquor trade through death and illness, which constantly depletes the staff of those employed. For this reason, the gradual reduc- tion in the number of licences proposed by the Bill will cause no appreciable displacement of labour ; while on the other hand it will most certainly stimu- late industry in other directions. (5) I come now to the question of Clubs, which is admittedly a difficalt problem, and as such has been hailed by opponents of the Bill as a convenient sort of stick with which to beat it. There aro certainly

great numbers of Clubs in this country conducted on respectable lines which are a convenience and advan- tage to the working class, and with which it would be a piece of downright folly and impertinence to inter- fere. Of course we shall not interfere with them. We shall guarantee every facility for the bona-fide social club, where the sale of drink for consumption by members is merely a convenient accessory, but on the other hand we wish to forestall attempts that might be made to multiply what are simply and solely drinking saloons. But I f;annot enter into detail on this subject which will need a great deal of very careful consideration, and probable revision in the Committee Stage, when I believe we shall find it can be quite well solved with- out real grievance in any quarter. TUB BUDGET.

And what am I to s.;;;Of-t-h-e-B.u-ciget introduced in a masterly speech of two hours or more this afternoon, to which I have already alluded. Surely this Budget is a landmark—and, I will say, a great laud-mark too (if only because it lays firmly anti final/if the foundations of OLD AGE PENSION-3 in tile financial history of our country. It has certainly placed Mr. Asquith on a footing with the greatest financiers in our political history. I do not envy the task of any one who tries to compress iato brief compass the statements, explanations and arguments, not only lucid and cogent, but already admirably compressed, in a speech by Mr. Asquith where every sentence tells, and where there is not a vestige of superfluous verbiage. I am sure that most of your readers will to-morrow be studying the speech for themselves, and if it should have escaped the attention of any friend of mine who does me the honour to real this letter, mty I respect- , fully recommend that speech to his attention. To my mind this speech by the Prime Minister,and the pamphlet issued by Sir Thomas Whittaker on the Licensing Question, of which I might mention that Tam in a few days sealing a number of copies to Warrington, are as well worth reading as anything just now in the hands of the public. So, in concluding this long letter, I will only just add that it would be impossible to exaggerate the unbounded satisfaction that one sees in the faces, and hears expressed about the Budget, by every man in our Party. Vours etc., A. H. CROSFIELD. London, May 7th, 1908.

div.head: VOTE ON LICENSING BILL.
div.p: VOTE ON LICENSING BILL.
SECOND READING CARRIED BY 248. A Warnini-i-c;—the Lords.
In the House of Commons on Mon;lay after furthet debate on the Licensing Bill, in -which Mr. Lloyd- Mr. Lc' lton, Mr. Arthur Henderson, Sir E.

George, ir. Lyttelton, Mr. SITLWA. Carson, and Mr. Asquith took part, the Opposition amendment against the second rending was negatived by 307 votes to 147—Government majority 250. A significant passage in the speech with which Mr. Asquith closed the debate pointed to the possibility, in the event of the ultimate loss of the Bill, of the inclusion in nest year's Budget of a scheme of high licence duties. LOCAL M.P.'S VOTES. Among those who voted for the second reading were Messrs. Asthury, 11. Bell, Sir Jim Brunner, J. F. L. Brunner, R.R. Cherry, 11. Cox, A. H. Crosfield, C. Seddon, Colonel Seely, D. Shackleton, P. Snoween, A. L. Stanley, Austin Taylor, J. Tonkinson, 11. Vivian, and A. Williamson. Included in the number who voted against the Bill - were Lord Balcarres, Messrs. Harmood Banner, W. C. Bridgeman, Sir Clement Bill, R. P. Houston, T. 11. W. Idris, Joynson-Hicks, C. IPArthur, Sir F. div.head: VISIT TO THE HOUSE.
div.p: A VISIT TO THE HOUSE.
BY MR. C. E. PARKER.

Last Monday night I got to the House of Commons about six o'clock aimed with a ticket which had been sent to me by our lember, accompanied with the request that I should be there at half-past two. Three and a half hours late I presented my ticket with all aseurance I could command, but the man in blue smiled and told me there were about forty who had ptecedence over me and I must wait my turn. I showed my disappointment. I do not know whether he recognized that I came from Warrington or whether some other mysterious influence or anticipation affected him, but lie came to the conclusion that full as the gallery was, somehow there would be room for a Warrington man. On settling to listen I was saluted by a familiar voice and recognized near me a friend of aldermanic standing, but not of circumference, of certain poetic ingenins, and of uncertain political tendencies. He told me that I had just missed a splendid speech by Lloyd-George. The debate was of great interest, but unevenly sustained. As a rule the speaking on the opposition side was rather of the apologetic style and lacked that strident outside note which finds expres- sion in confiscation and robbery. The froth had gone off. Lord Robert Cecil and others seemed to think it necessary to apologise for the intemperance of the Brewers' crusade. I was glad to hear one member (and an authority) speak up for the character of clubs. Perhaps about no Bill has there ever been so much exaggeration, and the exaggeration about the danger of Workmen's Clubs has been much overdone. No one has been able to associate in any general way the proportion of clubs, and the creation of clubs, with the diminution of licences. For example in those places where the public-houses alreody stand in the proportion of one to tho thousand there are no extra Lumber of work- men's clubs, and those that exist have a good record. Why, if public-houses were to be reduced to one in seven hundred, we should expect an increase of clubs merely for drinking purposes, I cannot see. Space forbids me to enlarge on the minor speeches and I must confine raysolf to the winding-up by Sir E. Carson on the one side and the Premier on the

other. Sir Edward made a number of good points and emphasized them in a solemn, almost tragic manner. He had a splendid audience, every seat being full downstairs, and there was an overflow of members to the galleries. Perhaps his most effective point, or rather I should perhaps say the point he made most effective, was in connection with the memorandum which had hwn issued by the inland Revenue in 1890, wherein a licence was treated in the succession duty accounts as " permanently enhanced by the licence." " When you want to get money out of the trade,"said Sir Edward, "you treat a licetu.e. as being permanently enhanced in value, but when it suits your purpose you treat the licence as being for one year." It did not seem to Tilt tba a case should be made to Kest ni.pe.n the two of 3 wad ill A ildemOranthiiii from The Inland nevenue, but in point of fact this memorandum was issued prior to the Sharpe v. Wake- field decision, and the matter was made perfectly clear by a memorandum from the same department which emphasized the sub-section five of section seven of the Finance -Act of 1891, namely, "the principal value of any property shall be estimated to be the price which in the opinion of tht commissioners such property would fetch if sold in the open market at the time of the death of the deceased." Surely the value of an estate is its realizable value, and the Inland Revenue department have nothing to do with the question of permanency; all they insist upon is succession duty on the value established by the public. Sir Edward gave us a full hour. Mr. Asquith replied in about twenty minutes. Perhaps the most significant feature in the reply was the way in which he combated the idea of con- ' fiscation, by suggesting that the monopoly value could be readily secured to the State by a simple process of charging the licensee yearly far the value of the licence. The Premier said : - The licensee of a public-house gets fifteen years' notice, and yet that is called confiscation ! tn a couple of days I shall have to bring in a Budget. Suppose I raise the present lieence duty from its present trumpery, illusory amount to a real, adequate and swinging duty. I am not going to do it, but would that be confiscation ? Or suppose this Bill does not pass, and next year my right hon. friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer creates an ascending scale of licence duties extending over ten years, would that be confiscation ? The Premier waited for a reply and if [located the " No " aright it came from young Austin who as an ex-Chancellor of the Exchequer often embarasses his own side by rushing in and giving the show away. The reply was obvious. How then can it be confisca- tion to give fourteen years free rent and only ask the licensees to pay the full rent at the end of the period?

"To Arms." A POEM BY THE LATE CHIEF CONSTABLE. At the present juncture the following poem from the pen of the late Chief Consmble (Mr. Luke Talbot) is of considerable interest. It appears in the current issue of " The Dawn." There's a ruler in the kingdom who is mighty as tho King, There's a tyrant who is worshipped as a god, Though the dungeon and the gibbet, where his sacrifices swing Mark the way of desolation he has trod. From the pauper's house of gloom, from the Bedlam's padded room, Cry the victims of his cruelty and wrong ; But he flourishes and thrives on a holocaust of lives, And this is his triumphant song— REFRAIN. Drink ! drink Hear the glasses chink ! Prison-gate and scaffold-rings are clanking in the clink ; Who can count my roll of slaves ? Or the lone, dishonoured graves Where the legions of the lost are laid for drink, drink, drink ? Come, my comrades, who will fight him for the freedom of the race— For our Mother England's honour and her life, For the homesteads that he harries, for the shrines he would deface, For the love of little children and the wife? We are Britain's burly eons, never far behind her guns When a foeman threatens danger from without ; Shall the traitor fight and win who has shed her blood within? Fling the standard to the skies and shout— Drink ! drink ! Hear the sabre clink ! We shall never sheathe it till your banners reel and sink; Till we've fought the fight and won, Till you're lying dead, and done, And the muffled drums are beating over drink, drink, drink !
LUKE TALBOT.

div.head: " Hell Laid Open." PATHETIC APPEAL IN LICENSING CASE.
div.p: " Hell Laid Open." PATHETIC APPEAL IN LICENSING CASE.

A pathetic cry for the poor was heard at the Glasgow Licensing Court, on Wednesday, when the justices had under consideration appeals against granting licences near Glasgow Docks. The seamen's representative caused a sensation by exclaiming : "For God's sake, and for the sake of the women and children, have mercy, and give the poor a chance to live ! " He characterised the district as " Hell laid open." The court, by nine to eight, granted the licence appealed against. Primitive Methodist Support.

At the annual Synod in connection with the Liverpool District of the Primitive Methodist Church held at Warrington on Saturday, it was resolved : In view of the tremendous efforts made by the supporters of the liquor traffic to defeat the Government Licensing Bill, we urge on all our churches the importance of organiz- ing outdoor and indoor meetings in support of it, the displaying of posters on the church notice boards and the holding of prayer meetings to entreat the blessing of God on the measure." IN THE ENEMY'S CITADEL. Probably the first resolution of any important assembly in Burton-on-Trent in favour of the Licensing Bill was carried on Monday by the members of the Primitive Methodist Synod for tha Nottingham district. The motion, which was declared carried unanimously as representing 30 churches and nearly a million mem- bers, adherents, and scholars, expressed gratitude to the Government for the Bill as a statesmanlike and courageous measure, and for regarding the welfare of the nation as of greater importance than the interests of a trade, and hoped that the Government would not be moved from their purpose by clamour.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication musnit all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith.

Veterans' Relief Fund. Sir,—May I through the columns of your valuable paper invite any lady interested in the welfare of the Veterans of Crimea and Indian Mutiny to attend a meeting at the Town Hall on Wednesday next the 13th instant at 3.30 p.m.? The Lady Mayoress of Liverpool (Mrs. Caton) will address the meeting and explain by what means funds may be raised to supplement the pension of those Veterans who are in need. I trust there will be a good attendance to assist in so worthy a cause.—Believe me, yours faithfully, JANE SMETHURST, Mayoresa. Town Hall, Warrington, Bth May 1503.

The Borough Accounts. Sir,—lleferring to the report of the Borough Treasurer presented to the Council last Tuesday, presumably on the instructions of a Committee, I consider a few corantentS arising out a the matter would at this juncture be opportune. \Vith regard to the late Mr. Brierle?, ItS he had no authority to receive or pay accounts, so far ad he was concerned there were no accounts to be audited by the Borough Auditors. : With respect to the Borough Treasurer's report lam quite in accord with it, believing it will lead to more effective control, and I am glad to see that the Council have adopted it. It is, however, obvious to the business men of the town that the Council should go an important step further, as it would be of considerable advantage to the interests of the Borough. The obvious step is this— That the whole of the accounts of the various depart- ments of the Corporation should be placed under the management and supervision of the Borough Treasurer and the whole of the receiving offices be centralised. This would not only be a great gain to the public con- venience; but I estimate would lead to a saving to the borough purse of at least £l,OOO a year. Other advan- tages would accrue, but I may sum them up in the worth: facilities, economical working and increased efficiency. There can be no question that if the Corporation undertakings were under the control of a private firm or a limited company a re-organisation on these lines would take place.—Yours faithfully, E. ENGLAND.
