div.head: TEMPERANCE QUEEN.
div.p: THE TEMPERANCE QUEEN.
BAND OF HOPE FESTIVAL AT THE PARR HALL.
A Pretty Spectacle.

With regal pomp and ceremony and the joyous acclaim of loyal subjects, the Temperance Queen was crowned at the Parr Ilan on Wednesday evening. It was a happy idea of the workers of the Warrington Band of Hope Union to thus welcome the advent of the " Merrse month." The festival had much in it that was reminiscent of the old-time revels—too rare in these utilitarian days —and one could hardly con- ceive of anything more pleasing than the sight of 350 ' children joining gaily and light-heartedly in the ' rejoicings which heralded the accession of the Temperance Queen. The enjoyment was by no means confined to the little ones, for the adults who assembled in such large numbers thoroughly entered into the spirit of the occasion and manifested apprecia- tion by frequent and cordial applause. To the accompaniment of martial strains on the organ, there was a precession round the hall and on to , the platform where the throne was in readiness for the coronation ceremony. Quite a medley of characters figured in the pageant. Personages famous in nursery rhyme and in history, representatives of the virtues, the seasons and different nacionalties—all were there. Of course, there was a portly John Bull accompanied by a dignified Britannia. Lord Roberts fraternized with Oliver Cromwell, and Charles L,Lord Nelson,Napoleon, and other notabilities of bye-gone days added distinc- tion to the festival. Last but by no means least came the suffragettes. They held aloft- mottos such as " Women's rights "and "United we stand " but they looked amiable enough and their appearance only created good-humoured laughter. As the processionists passed on to the platform the beauty of the scene Wes enhanced by the display of vane-coloured limelights. All having taken their places, the opening hymns "Courage Christian Soldier " was heartily sung. Prayer having been offered by the Bev. J. B. Buglass and a brief address delivered by Mrs. Dodds, the President of the Union, the stirring chorus " Hail, Festal Day " was given in admirable style. The audience had then to imagine that the platform was for the nonce transformed into a village green and a band of happy youngsters indulged in leap-frog, "jolly miller," skipping and other garnee with as much enthusiasm as if the sport were quite spontaneous. Then came the great event of tha evening—the croening ceremony. The retiring queen (Minnie Whitmore), wearing a beautiful floral crown and attended by maids of honour and train bearers, entered with due stateliness and was escorted to the throne which, as if by a magic touch, at once became brilliantly illuminated with electric lights. The Queen having announced that her term of office was now over, the choice of a sucessor engaged attention and the rival claims of Purity, Courage, Love, Faith, Hope and Charity for the honour wore eloquently pleaded. While the multitude was in doubt as to whom to select the fairy queen appeared and bade them choose Temperance as Queen of the May—and they immediately did as commanded, femperance being elected with loud cheers. A few lines in the retiring Queen's valedictory address neatly expressed the sentiment of the moment : " The Light is spreading o'er the world, Gospel ministers fight more loyally against the drink ; magistrates, in fuller wisdom, reject the brewers' plans ; and Parliament has promised to protect the children—and save the race." The retiring Queen was then divested of her fleral crown and placed it on the head of the new Queen (May Isherwood) whose appearance on the throne WM welcomed with the chorus "Hail to the Queen of May." Then the revels began. A group of little girls,daintily dressed, gave the maypole dance very cleverly,and much praise is due to Mrs. Whitmore who hid trained them. Priscilla Cottoril sweetly sang " Water from the Spring," the choir joining in the chorus. A delightful fairy dance, for which some of the girls had been trained by Miss Spinks, followed and proved one of the most successful features of the entertainment,the pretty costumes of the girls and the charming way in which they tripped about combining to produce an effective picture. The humorous element was well to the fore, and the action song "The Wackenfufen Band " by senior boys (trained by Mr. Spruce) was an undoubted hit, the grotesque antics of these nondescript musicians creating laughter loud and long. The old-time Morris dance was splendidly executed by some lads and lasses who had been trained by Mr. W. Aldred, and met with enthusiastic appreciation. A duet and chorus "A lament and prayer " was a pleasing item, Arthur Weir and Ben Farrar singing their parts in a highly creditable manner. The action song " The child and the butterfly " by junior girls (trained by Mrs. Whitmore) afforded a charming spectacle, the youthful performers being beautifully costumed and singing well. The duet "You needn't be so stuck up," in which a well-to-do girl insinuates her superiority over a less-fortunate sister, but is brought to sea the error of her waye, the two becoming great friends., was tastefully interpreted by Elsie Whitfield and Dolly Caine, and took the fancy of the audience. A Dutch dance by girls irs the national dress, complete with. sabots, was capably performed ! and delighted everyone. Miss Spinks was responsible , for their training. A part song Whispering winds " was rendered with taste and expression by a select choir. A very amusing action song "The policeman" by junior boys (trained by Master B. Spruce) added considerably to the interest of the programme, the valiant defenders of the peace taking the unusual le—for such songs— of extolling the joys of the policeman's lot. A mandoline solo was pleasingly given by Sophia Clatworthy who was warmly applauded for her Lskill. A tuneful duet " The night bells " by Jessie Woodland and Hilda Spruce was creditably interpreted. Then came the most original feature of the entertain- ment, showing that the eromotors are nothing if not up-to-date. It was an action song "The suffragettes " in which senior girls (trained by Mrs. Davenport) took part. They appeared on the stage bearing cards inscribed ! with their war cries and proceeded in song to denounce mere man and proclaim woman's right to the vote and even to sit in Parliament. Between the verses their leader (Miss J.Ellison) harangued the crowd which was supposed to have assembled and hurled choice ePithet Pligb 08 "unmitigated numskull," at the n!ale-kind. The incident finished true to life, a contingent of youthful police storming the platform and hnstling VA() Inpleii eliffragettel away from their meeting place. The last deuce on the pro- gtitrense was one of the most beautiful—" :Morrie England "—and was given with admirable effect by girls trained by Miss Spinks. A budding humorist—J. Nurse—took the house by storm with the song "He ! Ha ! Ha ! " His confidence and self-possession eminently fitted him for the item and its humour could not have been better brought out. The entertainment which had been successful in the highest degree from beginning to end closed with the inspiring chorus " Stand fast for the glory of freedom.' Too much praise cannot be accorded to the workers who must have been untiring in their efforts to produce such happy results. They had their reward in knowing that , the entertainment provided real pleasure for the audience , and, no doubt, in equal measure to the children who figured in it with so much pride. Mr. A. IV. Clatworthy ! presided at the organ with taste and skill, and Mr. A. Spruce was a capable conductor. The duties of pianists were discharged dy Misses Lomas, Fellows, Spruce and Plinston. It should be moo- tinned that the children had been trained for the village green sports by Mesdames Davenport, Whitmore and Shaw, and Messrs. Whitfield and Fellows and for the crowning ceremony by Mesdames Whitmore and rrai steu,la specialttna I r etchoeg ocni aism must s thDheae madevseuncpcoeorstfs. the devoted dhh lveeonetteoedni abours of Mr. F. Gandy AS hon. ecretary. He had two able assistants in Messrs. Henry Woolley and J. Muir. The committee was composed of the following :—Messrs. T. Dale, It. P. Williams, G. Whitfield, J. P. Jackson, A. Spruce, A. Clatworthy, Hamblett, G. Colley, B. Littlewood, C. S. Fellows, E. Taylor, J. Howell, B. Spruce, and W. Aldred, :Mesdames Whitmore, Unsworth, Davenport, Firth, Shaw and J. Shaw, Misses Edwards, Whalley, Clayton, Ellison, Ormistou and Plinston. Mr. G. Whitfield was an efficient platform manager and director of elocution and Mr. C. S. Fellows marshalled the procession.

div.head: CAUSES FOR ENCOURAGEMENT.
div.p: CAUSES FOR ENCOURAGEMENT.

Mrs. Dorms, the President of the Union, presided over the festival, and in the course of a brief address said that since they last met on a similar occasion a battle cry had been sounded and men and women, irrespective of creed and politics, had buckled on the armour and joined in the fight. It was a wonder- ful army, including old men who had been fighting for many years, and who now hoped to seo the fruits of their labour, old men and matrons, young men and maidens, and last hut not least the noble army of children which they called the Band of Hope. And so they moved on, " Strong in the Lord and in the power of His might," and they trusted that as those children grew up they would keep true to their Band of Hope pledges, so tbat when the time came for the present leaders to lay down the weapons of warfare the young people would be ready to take their places. They must take heart of grace and go on rejoicing, " Strong in the Lord of Hosts, And in His mighty Power ; Who in the strength of Jesus trusts Is more than conqueror."—(Applause.) A VETERAN WORKER.

Mrs. OwEv, of Penketh, on behalf of the British Women's Temperance Association,presented a beautiful bouquet to the retiring Queen. In doing so she said she believed sho was the oldest band of hope girl in the hall that night, her pledge card being signed on December 21th, 1831. She had always kept that pledge and she had always belonged to the band of hope, and she loved band of hope children. She hoped all the young people present that night would keep their pledges and become earnest temperance workers. (Applause.) Later Mrs. On presented the new Queen with a Bible.

SPEECH BY THE EX-LORD 11IAYOR OF MANCHESTER. The proceedings on Thursday evening, when the pro- gramme was repeated, were even more successful than Wednesday's festival, the hall being crowded in every part. Councillor John Harrop, Lord Mayor of Man- chester 1900-7 and the first Band of Hope member to attain this distinction, presided. The hymn "Courage, Christian soldier " having been sung. the Rev. A. 51. Mitchell, vicar of Bartonwool, offered prayer. The CliAirtm AN congratulated the parents upon the pleasing and healthy appearance of the children he saw on the platform. At present, he continued, the country was very much agitated with regard to the legislation which his Majesty's Government had thought fit to introduce. but he was not going to deal with the measure that night, because if it were passed—and he felt sure it would be—(applause)—there would be 60,000 public-houses and bear-houses still left to be dealt with. They were all agreed that there was too much drunkenness in this country and too many people were ruined every year through the curse of intemperance. They were also agreed that the largest amount of insanity was brought about by indulgence in drink and that the filling of our gaols, lunatic asylums and workhouses and a great deal of unemployment were largely the result.of intemperance. One of England's greatest statesmen said that our deurikenness accounted for more deaths than war, pestilence and famine combined. That was a saying of the late Mr. Gladstone—(applause)—and when he Spoke ha spoke with authority. It was when they came to apply the remedy that they differed, but there could be no two opinions with regard to bringing up the child in , the way it should go. (Applause). When a child was brought up to shun the drink, and live a sober life, they could depend upon it that when he became a citizen or I a townsman he would have a faith within him and would know why he was a teetotaller ore temperance reformer. It might be an encouragement to some of the boys present if he told them that fifty years ago he came to the conclusion that he would neither touch,taste nor handle drink as long as God gave him breath—(applause)--and he had been trying in his little way for many years to persuade children to follow that example. In the War- rington Band of Hope Union, connected as it was with some twenty-six different Sunday schools, he believed there were about 5,009 children—(applause)—who in a few years would become citzens and take the places of the workers who would then be no more. He was pleased to note that the Prima Minister in his Budget speech that day had said that notwithstanding that there was an increase in the revenue from strong drink in theyears 1903 and 1937 there was a decrease of £lOO,OOO this year. (Applause.) The nation was bound to become more sober because attention was being called to the evils of drink on every baud and influences were at work which would benefit this town, the nation and the people generally. Let them rise up with the voice of one man and do what they could to sweep the curse from the land. (Applause.) Cycling. That full advantage was taken of the glorious weather which prevailed last Saturday was proved by the fact that over thirty members of the Warrington Cycling Club took part in the Club run to Acton Bridge, where tea was partaken of at the Railway Hotel, some of the members afterwards indulging in bowls, and altogether a most enjoyable day being spent. On Tuesday. the opening night run of the season was carried out, the roads which were in a wretched condition, greatly affecting the turnout. However, some fifteen members eventually landed at Sankey Chapel House after a circular ride, and an impromptu smoker was held. To-day the members will be in full force at Runcorn, where a festival is being held on behalf of local charities.

Bowling. I Saturday was an ideal day for bowlers and there was 'a large gathering of enthusiasts on Rylands' Recreation Ground in Gorsey-lane to witness the match between • twenty-five members at Rylands' club and twenty-five ' players representing the Warrington and District Bowling Association. The proceeds were in aid of the Infirmary. Messrs. Rylauds vvorkpeople are to be con- gratulated upon having secured such a fine recreation ground which is being laid out to the best possible ' advantage. Already there are three splendidly-laid bowling greens, each forty yards square, and a fourth is ! contemplated. A spacious pavilion, to cost £3,000, is ; in course of erection and when completed will be one of the best in the district. Mr. Percy Silcock is the architect and Mr. Warburton the builder.

Songs were rendered during the evening by Messrs. T. Humphreys, W. W. Whittle, Victor Roberts, G. Barnes and W. Dennett, and were highly appreciated. Mr. Fred Wolfenden presided at the piano. div.head: -o--- WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: -o--- WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL
Re-Election of Chairman.

The annual meeting of this Council was held at the Bewsey Chambers on Wodaesday when there were present : Dr. Murray, Messrs. A. Brooks, J. Ball, J. Mather, J. Backhouse, W. Furness, W. Stanier, R. ForshaNv, J. C. Sutton (clerk), B. S. Newcombe (sur- veyor), Dr. Sephton (medical otiicer), and F.W. Kerfoot (inspector).

div.head: EtECTXONS.
div.p: EtECTXONS.

The Clerk was appointed chairman pro tent. Mr. Baooxs moved that Dr. Murray be appointed chairman for the ensuing year. He need not ask whether Dr. Murray had done his duty or not. Mr. Fonsitlw seconded and the resolution was carried unanimously. Dr, MITRIt.U' than took the chair and expressed his thanks. He said he hoped that at the end of the year he would be able to merit their appreciation again: Mr. J. BILL moved that Mr. Forshaw be appointed vice-chairman. He said that Dr. Murray had not loft much for Mr. Forshaw to do, but if there was anything to do Mr. Forshavv would do it.

Mr. MATHER seconded, the CHAIMIAN supported and the resolution was carried. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. SEPIITON reported that the deaths numbered 41 (12 males and 20 females) ; the births numbered • 40, (19 males and 21 females). The excess of births over deaths was nil. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 331 per thousand, against 25 the average of the last three months, and against 235 the corresponding month last year. Thirty deaths occurred at Winwick Asylum. The death-rate proper for the district equalled 10.5 per thousand of the population. During the month three cases of scarlet fever had occurred ; diptheri a, seven cases ; and erysipelas two oases. The repart was adopted. The CIIAIRMAN moved that Dr. Sephton and Mr. lierfoot be re-appointed medical officer of health and nuisance inspector respsctively. Mr. MATHEa seconded and the motion was carried.

TLIE EFFECT OF LAMPS, Mr. MATIIER said that for yoars and years when Manchester-road was a main road there wore no lamps and nothing happened. Now that it was thickly popu- lated and lamps were provided, burglaries had taken place. Mr. BP.OOKS : They can sea to do it. (Laughter). The CruastN: Do you suggest more lamps so that there cart be more burglaries? (Laughter). The subject then dropped.

div.head: WHITE CITY.
div.p: THE WHITE CITY.

The weather during the past few days in Manchester has been anything but favourable for outside working, nevertheless rapid progress has been made in the work of reconstruction at the White City. Those who visited this beautiful and popular pleasure resort last year will find very many important altera- tions have taken place, and Mr. J. Calvin Brown, Managing Director of the White City has never relaxed his efforts to make the White City the most up-to-date pleasure park in Europ3. The group of Bontoo Igorrates who arrived in Man- chester a few days back in the charge of Captain Mcßae,late of the Philippine Constabulary, aro working energetically building their village which occupies more than one acre of ground. The exhibition those barbarians give will be found to bo one of the most interesting and instructive ever witnessed in England, and it is pleasant to learn there will b 3 noQiing of an objectionable nature in their performance. The new Scenic Railway affords p assengers a ride of more than one mile through beautiful scenery and will undoubtedly attract thousands of amusement seekers. Among other novel features are a Water Chute, the highest and longest of its kind in England. America Negro dancers and stagers, Ye Oldo English Milk, &a. Basses-o'-th'-Barn Rand has been engaged fur the opening week and will give concerts during the after- noon and evening. The White City opens on Saturday May 16th and it is safe to predict a huge crowd will wend their way White Citywards on that day. .
If you are not as well as you would like to be try a tonic. H. M. Ashton's Life Tonic is the ideal tonic, Is. per bottle from H ASHTON,6I, Sankey- at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
VISIT OF THE BESSES OTH' BARN BAND

An important engagement has been made for to-morrow (Sunday), when two sacred concerts will be given by the above celebrated band, in the Palace Theatre and Hippodrome, at three and 7.45 p.m. This will not be the first visit of the band to Warrington,but it will no doubt attract a large audience on each occa- sion, as their performance is one which never fails to please. This is one of the finest brass bands in the world not merely on account of its successes in contests, bat because its work has received the hall-mark of approval from many of the most notable musicians of the day, men who are not, as a rule, favourably inclined towards brass band music, but who have been compelled to admit the thoroughly artistio standard of playing reached by the Basses o'tif Barn. Every member is a skilled musician, trained to the ' highest pitch of perfection in the performance of brass band music, and for precision in execution, accuracy in tune, purity and quality of tone, and expression the band have no superiors among brass combinations the world over. The band has travelled in many countries, and always with success. It scored an especial triumph in Paris, and this was particularly ple.ising, as it was feared the band might not meet with the favour of the Parisians, because they are accustomed to very large brass bands of from 50 to 60 players, nearly double the usual number of an English Band. But the Parisians learned that mere numbers do not moan everything, and that a band of from 30 to 31 skilled performers can produce quite sufficient volume of tone, and concerts given by the Besses took Paris by storm. NEXT WEEK'S ATTRACTION. Next week the management announce a special attraction in the shape of Fred ainnett's company who will appear in an improved edition of the .ever-popular and romantic eluestriart spectacle " Turpires Ride to York.

div.head: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
div.p: WARRINGTON BRIDGE.
A New Scheme Under Consideration.

A meeting of the Bridges Sub-C-immittee of the General Purposes Committee was held at the Town Hall on Thursday when the objections made to the proposed cantileveis for the widening of Warrington Bridge were considered.. We understand that a new scheme for the construction of a flat girder bridge resting on columns to be erected in the river and having a clear centre spin of about 60 feet was dis- cussed and the Through Surveyor was instructed to report thereon. . I SUGAR 15DEARER.—Advt.

div.head: LOCAL ART EXHIBITION.
div.p: LOCAL ART EXHIBITION.
To be Opened by Mr. A. H.
Crogield, M.P.

On Tuesday afternoon next Mr. A. H. Crosfield,. M.P. will open a memorial exhibition of tha works, of the late George Sheffield in the Warrington Art Gallery. Though he did not receive his art training here, Mr. Sheffield had very close associations with the town, and the exhibition will doubtless arouse considerable interest. It will consist of about 139 works in oil, pastel, water colour, sepia and black and white, including some of the finest specimens of his art. Amongst the contributors to the collection are Mr. A. H. Ctoshleld, MP., who is a well known connoisseur of Sneffield's work, Dr. Shipman, M.E'. (Northampton), Mr. Charles Elmondsoa (St. Annes- on-Sea), Mr. Abel Heywood (Manchester), Mr. G. W. Bullock (Bowdon), and many local owners. Mr. Crosfield will perform the opening ceremony (to which admiss;on will be by invitation) at 3.30, and Alderman Bennett (chairman of the Museum Committee) will preside.
The exhibition will be open to the public from Wednesday next to June Gth.

div.p: Y Branch of the B W.T.A.

A general meeting was held in connection with tha above at the Winmarlegh Cafe on Tuesday night. Miss Beswick presided. The Rev. J. F. Matthews gave a very eloquent address to the members, full of good advice with helpful suggestions for the coming , season. He also expressed his delight at the good : being done at the Silver-street Girls' Club and hoped it would continue to flourish. A musical programme was tastefully arranged, Miss Nelly Littlevrood open- ing with a pianoforte solo. Miss Griffiths followed with a song entitled "The magic month of May." A delighful recitation was given by Miss Porshaw, and encored. Miss Hibbert and Miss' Griffiths sang a charming duet. Twenty-two new members were enrolled.

Edwards b Dargan 1 Ireland not out 0 Extras 2 Extras Total -- CHURCH AND PEOPLE. Christianity Increases and Churchgoers Decrease. Preaching in Kensington Baptist Church, Liverpool, on Sunday evening, the Rev. Herbert Dunnico said that, while the interest in religion craving for intellectual certitude was greater than ever, the Church was certainly losing its hold upon the masses of the people. Mr. Philip Snowden had stated that the young men of intellect and grit were leaving the Churches because they misrepresented Jesus Christ ; that men were not outside the Churches because they had too little, but too I much, religion. Be (Mr. Dunnico) was not pre- pared to accept that version without much reservation ; but one thing seemed obvious—that while Christianity was increasing Chnrchianity was decreasing. The two things were not synonymous, but they ought certainly to go band in band. It was a real disaster when they were alienated. Mr. Dunnico remarked that, among many causes for the arrested progress of the Church, there could be no doubt that it was in some measure due to the atmosphere of the Churches. They were not democratio enough, and had apparently forgotten that the Great Founder was a common man, born of common people. The day had I gone when the Church could• afford to patronise the people. Every day added to the power of the people. The whole trend of politics was towards fuller emanci- pation, rod if the Church wished to retain its hold upon the people it must be free from caste and frankly , democratic. They had come to the parting of the ways. I The Church had to make its choice.
